#828. Bryce Dallas Howard Reacts to Robert Pattinson's James Bond Casting

Bryce Dallas Howard had the best reaction to her Twilight costar Robert Pattinson being named the new James Bond in an exclusive interview with E! News at the 2026 ELLE Women in Hollywood Celebration.

Robert Pattinson, you better hold on tight, spider monkey.

Because after being selected as the new James Bond following a yearslong search, his super stardom is about to reach new heights. But his Twilight costar Bryce Dallas Howard knew he had something special from the start.

“He's a sweetheart,” Howard exclusively told E! News’ Lauren Herbert at the 2026 ELLE Women in Hollywood Celebration in Beverly Hills, Calif., Nov. 16. “He had worked prior to Twilight, but Twilight was really sort of his breakthrough role.”

“And the whole time, at least when I worked with him, he was so sincere and sweet and just the loveliest guy, like not into stardom or himself or anything,” she added. “Just an incredibly present person.”

While Pattinson’s Edward Cullen may have killed Howard’s Victoria in the 2010 film The Twilight Saga: Eclipse—which also starred Kristen Stewart and Taylor Lautner—there’s certainly no bad blood.

“He decapitated me,” the Jurassic World: Dominion star quipped. “Privilege and honor to be decapitated by Robert Pattinson.”

That’s because of the person Pattinson, 40, was when he wasn’t wearing the skin of a killer.

“He’s not schmoozy,” Howard explained. “He’s not trying to be cool. He's just who he is, and he happens to be absolutely gorgeous. But he's a true artist, and his career since Twilight has obviously demonstrated that a zillion times over.”

So, though Jack Lowden, Callum Turner, Jacob Elordi, and Damson Idris were just a few stars who were rumored to be the next 007, it was The Odyssey actor who ultimately got the call to star in the new film helmed by his Dune: Part Three director Denis Villeneuve.

As Howard, 45, put it, “Him as James Bond feels really right.”

But the Primetime star is just one celeb getting their flowers from The Help star. After all, Howard presented Inde Navarrette with the Ralph Lauren Spotlight Award at the event.

"I don't even know who to liken her to because what she did is so utterly unique and singular,” Howard said, “I mean she's worked before Obsession, but Obsession is really her breakout role, and she arrived so fully formed.”

“It’s almost like Marilyn Monroe or something or Audrey Hepburn,” she continued. “She's an absolute icon already.”

Until Pattinson dominates the big screen as James Bond, keep reading to sink your teeth into Twilight’s best kept secrets…

1. When first writing Twilight, screenwriter Mark Lord recalled fears that the male audience wouldn't be interested. They wanted to take the concept of Romeo and Juliet, but with vampires "and build in a structure that was far more a cinematic structure," he shared on The Big Hit Show podcast in January 2022. "And they wanted to just put in more action to advance it more and give something more for the male audience. They thought they were going to lose the male audience with too much of a romance."

2. Director Catherine Hardwicke quickly made the writers pivot after throwing the first draft into the trash. "The original script literally had Bella on jet skis being chased by the FBI," she recalled. "She was a star athlete. Nothing to do with the book."

3. Paramount and MTV initially had acquired the film rights to Twilight, with the original script making significant changes to the book. "It had veered very far from the book, and so I did not like it at all," director Hardwicke revealed to CinemaBlend. After three years, Paramount released the rights and then-independent film studio Summit Entertainment immediately picked them up.

4. Book author Stephenie Meyer had some strict guidelines when it came to the adaptation of her source material. She didn't want any stereotypical vampire elements added in and demanded that Edward's "so the lion fell in love with the lamb" line make it into the final version.

She also stepped in to have Kellan Lutz take over the role of Emmett when she didn't agree with the initial casting choice and asked to have Bella and Edward's first kiss toned down. Of stepping in to put her foot down, Meyer told EW, "That's hard for me, but I'm glad of every time I did it and I don't think I stepped on too many toes and everyone seems to still like me."

5. According to Summit's then-Head of Production Erik Feig, Meyer was adamant that her vampires didn't have fangs. "The negotiated language says, 'No actor playing a vampire will have canine incisors longer than those found in the average human being,'" he recalled on Spotify's The Big Hit Show podcast. "And that to me is... I love that line."

6. Some soon-to-be-major actresses (including some who would become faces of their own respective franchises) that auditioned for Bella Swan included Emily Browning (Meyer's early first choice), Michelle Trachtenberg, Lily Collins and Jennifer Lawrence.

"I didn't really know what it was," Lawrence later said on The Howard Stern Show of her Twilight audition. "You just get like five pages [at the audition] and they're like, 'Act monkey.' And when it came out I was like, 'Hot damn. Whoa!'"

7. Based on a suggestion from Emile Hirsch, who starred opposite Kristen Stewart in Into the Wild and was in director Hardwicke's Lords of Dogtown, the filmmaker zeroed in on Stewart for the role.

"I see Kristen…with all that longing and just lusting for Emile [Hirsch] And I'm like, 'Oh my God, that is so what I felt from the book. This girl that has so much longing, and it's so contained, and just repressed longing, but it was so palpable,'" Hardwicke said of watching Stewart in Into the Wild. "So I thought, 'Oh, it's got to be Kristen.'"

8. The actress initially had no interest in the project upon hearing the synopsis, but after meeting with Hardwicke and going through the script together, Stewart quickly changed her mind.

9. Over 5,000 actors reportedly went out for the role of Edward Cullen, including Dave Franco, Jamie Campbell Bower (who would go on to play Caius in the follow-up films), Schitt's Creek's Dustin Milligan and Michael Welch (who landed the role of human Michael Newton). Moreover, Henry Cavill was Meyer's first choice, but was too old by the time the movie came along. He was reportedly considered for the role of Carlisle, the Cullen family patriarch.

But the final four contenders were Robert Pattinson, Ben Barnes, Shiloh Fernandez and Jackson Rathbone (who would eventually nab the role of Jasper Cullen), and they were all brought to Hardwicke's home in California to test opposite Stewart.

10. The chemistry read involved the infamous meadow scene, which Stewart and Pattinson performed on Hardwicke's bed. When it came to the kiss, Hardwicke recalled Pattinson being a bit too revved-up, but told EW, "It was electric." Pattinson later revealed he took half a Valium before the make-or-break audition.

After the four actors tested, Hardwicke was still uncertain, but Stewart knew who her Edward was right away, telling Vanity Fair, "I was like, "'Are you kidding me!? It's such an obvious choice!'"

11. Prior to landing Twilight, Pattinson had considered leaving the entertainment industry after a string of failed auditions following Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (RIP Cedric Diggory!). "I was going to quit [acting] because I never got any jobs," he would recall on Today, "so I guess it's not really quitting when you're not getting jobs—it's just surrendering to fate."

12. While he would go on to play the titular teen wolf in MTV's hit series Teen Wolf, Tyler Posey revealed he auditioned against his good friend Taylor Lautner for the role of Jacob Black in the first film. "So, yeah, I auditioned for Twilight, Jacob Black. Taylor Lautner beat me," he told MTV with a laugh. "Congratulations, dude. That's a sick role. That's awesome. I hate you."

13. Another young star who auditioned for a role in Twilight was future Pretty Little Liars actress Lucy Hale who wanted to play Alice Cullen (she would also audition for Jane in New Moon and Leah Clearwater in Eclipse). She told J-14, "I read the books and I wanted to be part of the first movie so bad."

14. After initially going out for the role of villain James, Cam Gigandet (known for his bad boy turn on The O.C.) was brought back in to read for Emmett Cullen. "So I was like, 'Is there anything you guys have for me? Anything at all?' And so I went in for Kellan Lutz's character," he told MTV. "Once I went in, I was like, 'Oh my gosh, I like this character, but I just have to play James.' We waited a little bit, and after about a week, we heard back, and they were like, 'OK, we'll give him the job.'"

15. Meyer made a brief cameo in the first film as one of the diners in a scene between Bella and her dad Charlie (Billy Burke). She would also appear in Breaking Dawn: Part 1 as a guest as Bella and Edward's wedding, along with screenwriter Melissa Rosenberg, co-producer Bill Bannerman and producer Wyck Godfrey.

16. "On the first shot on the first day I strained one of my ass cheeks, my ass just couldn't take the strain of the first one," Pattinson revealed to Jimmy Kimmel . His injury caused a problem with the company insuring the film and led to a bit of physical therapy for the star.

17. When New Moon was officially announced the day after Twilight dominated its opening night at the box office, fans were shocked to see Lautner not listed among the cast members. But it wasn't a typo, as the studio confirmed it was assessing whether or not the 16-year-old could play the character after his wolf transformation.

"The doubts came up because he had very few scenes in the first movie, and also because he's described as being 6-foot-5 in the second book, so there were reasonable facts that we had to come to grips with," New Moon director Chris Weitz explained to Reuters of the 5-foot-9 star.

18. In fact, there was even an actor in mind to take over the part: The Scorpion King 2 and One Tree Hill star Michael Copon. "I have nothing against Taylor personally. I think he's great and tremendous at what he does," Copon told MTV. "But it's just adjusting to the fact that Jacob has to grow. It's a matter of going with the storyline."

19. But Lautner was committed to playing Jacob, taking on an intense training regime to bulk up as soon as production wrapped on the first film. His prep included consuming 4,000 calories per day, eating every two hours and working out for two hours at least five days a week.

"I knew I had to get to work right away; there could be no waiting involved," the then-17-year-old told Interview. "The day I finished Twilight, I came home and started bulking up. For New Moon, I'm 30 pounds heavier than I was in Twilight."

20. While Lautner (and his legions of fans) enjoyed his physical transformation, there was one aspect to playing Jacob that the actor didn't like: that wig. "There was hatred between both of us," he told MTV. "It did not like me, I did not like it. Not fond memories."

21. After dyeing her hair blonde to play Cullen family member Rosalie in the first film, Nikki Reed opted to wear a wig for the rest of the series to protect her hair. "My hair fell out," she revealed to MTV of the damage. "It took 36 hours initially to make me blond, and every other day, I was bleaching my head and my skin. This time around, we are testing out different wigs and stuff."

22. More wig woes: After cutting her hair to play Joan Jett in The Runaways, Stewart had to wear a wig for Eclipse, one that earned a lot of eyebrow-raises. Leading up to Breaking Dawn: Part 1, Stewart assured fans she would be rocking her own hair and revealed Summit really didn't want her to chop her hair in the first place.

"They're going to hate me for this, but they offered me lots of ridiculous... many ridiculous things to not do that," she told George Lopez in 2010. "I completely understand, I just thought we'd have a better...wig, and, uh, it's OK, we worked it out, and hopefully, hopefully, hopefully, it's OK now."

23. After originating the role of villain vamp Victoria, Rachelle Levefre was replaced by Bryce Dallas Howard (who was first approached to take on the role years prior) in Eclipse. And Levefre was not happy about the casting change, which the studio attributed to scheduling conflicts.

"I was stunned by Summit's decision to recast the role," Levefre said in a statement. "I was fully committed to the Twilight saga, and to the portrayal of Victoria."

24. Newcomer Xavier Samuel won the role of Riley, Victoria's sidekick, in the franchise's third installment, reportedly beating out Channing Tatum and Harry Potter star Tom Felton for the job.

25. Michael Sheen took on the role of Volturi coven leader Aro because his daughter Lily (with Kate Beckinsale) was a massive fan of the series. "I was mainly excited about it because I knew I would make my daughter very happy," he told The Daily Record. "That was the main reason, and then I read the books and I really enjoyed them. I didn't think I was going to, but I really did."

26. For Bella's highly anticipated wedding dress, production turned to Carolina Herrera. "Carolina had worked with Stephenie personally for events. And they'd struck up a friendship and dialogue so we talked to Carolina for the dress," costume designer Michael Wilkinson revealed to MTV. "They'd been talking about the day that this dress would hit the big screen for a while and I was happy to help with the design as a consultant because it had to work with the rest of the film."

For the rest of the Cullen women and Bella's mom, the costume designer created original dresses for each character.

27. The problem with a custom couture wedding gown? The chances were high of it getting ruined—which almost happened due to the bad weather in Oregon—and they only had two duplicates.

"I had a vision of the wet paint slowly creeping up the hem of the dress, but in the end, we got away with it," Wilkinson told InStyle. "We shot the wide shot first, and sure enough, by the time we moved in for the close-ups, the hem was soaking up the paint like a thirsty sponge!"

28. Okay, but how did Edward get Bella pregnant when he's, you know, dead, and she's not? Meyer actually provided an answer to this question on her official website back in the day: "Like with vampire skin—which looks similar to human skin and has the same basic function—fluids closely related to seminal fluids still exist in male vampires, which carry genetic information and are capable of bonding with a human ovum." So there you go.

29. The original cut of Bella and Edward's wedding night sex scene initially caused Breaking Dawn: Part 1 to receive an R-rating, with director Bill Condor forced to tone down the couple's highly awaited first time. "There are very specific guidelines on thrusting intercourse," he told The Hollywood Reporter.

30. Pattinson nearly caused the fanbase to combust in 2011 when he revealed at a press conference for Breaking Dawn that a real priest was used for the wedding scene, "So technically we are already married because he did all the things you would do in a normal ceremony," he explained. "So we don't have a civil union in law, but I guess in the church we are actually married."

31. After Stewart wore a B.B. Dakota coat in the first film, the clothing company rebranded it as "the Bella Swan jacket." Summit swiftly filed a legal claim and in 2011, a judge ruled in their favor.

32. Stars you may have forgotten appeared in the franchise's films include Anna Kendrick, Shameless' Noel Fisher, Lost star Maggie Grace, Lee Pace, Westworld's Angela Sarafyan and Oscar winner Rami Malek. In fact, Kendrick kind of forgot she was in the series. "Holy s--t," she tweeted in 2018. "I just remembered I was in Twilight."

33. In an interview with Vulture years later, Hardwicke didn't exactly have fond memories of her time reading the scripts for Twilight, admitting, "Every one of those scripts sucked. Oh Lord, did they suck." She isn't the only franchise director to bash the series, with David Slade having to apologize for disparaging comments he made before signing on to direct Eclipse. "Twilight drunk? No, not even drunk. Twilight on acid? No, not even on acid? Twilight at gun point? Just shoot me," he once said during a radio interview.

34. A 10 year-old Mackenzie Foy landed the integral role of Renesmee, Bella and Edward's half-vampire half-human baby that Jacob imprints on (LOL remember that?). And the entire production team and cast were protective of the newcomer on the set of Breaking Dawn: Part 2. To protect the tween, director Condor placed a swear jar on set (it accumulated more than $800!) and the two leads went just a bit meta.

"They were amazing with her," Condor told EW. "It really brought something paternal out in Rob, and Kristen was especially protective. I'd have to interrupt them when they were in deep conversation to get going with a scene."

While CGI was ultimately used to portray the baby version of Renesmee, it was later revealed the production team attempted to use a doll to extremely creepy results. Seriously, it earned the nickname Chuckesmee.

#827. Romario demands Ancelotti sacking as war of words continues

Few would have predicted that Carlo Ancelotti would be facing the wrath of a Brazil legend just 18 months into his tenure as head coach of the national team.

But Romario, Brazil's fourth-highest scorer behind only Neymar, Pele and Ronaldo, has publicly demanded legendary manager Ancelotti be relieved of his duties twice in the past week.

It all started after Brazil suffered a 3-2 friendly defeat by Japan on Friday thanks to a controversial stoppage-time winner from Tatsuhiro Sakamoto.

Ancelotti received a red card for dissent in the aftermath - the first of his international management career, as Barcelona forward Raphinha also saw red.

And after Brazil's friendly defeat, Romario took to social media to air his frustrations about the former Real Madrid boss.

"Ancelotti, enough is enough! Pack your bags and leave!" he wrote on Instagram.

"Nobody questions your history. You are one of the greatest coaches world football has ever seen, but that was at club level."

Brazil were eliminated by Norway in the last 16 at the 2026 World Cup, meaning they failed to qualify for the quarter-finals for the first time since 1990.

And Romario alluded to this too, stating the country "can't take the risk of throwing another World Cup in the trash - the time to act is now!"

The Brazil boss has been in the game long enough to know how to deal with all sorts of opinions.

Ancelotti has won the Champions League a record five times as a head coach and won the league title in all of Europe's top five divisions, along with multiple domestic cups.

But his record with Brazil is far from perfect. Across 21 matches, they have recorded 12 wins, four draws and five defeats.

However, while Ancelotti acknowledges the need for improvement, he emphasised the fact that it is still "a new project".

Speaking before Brazil's friendly with Singapore on Tuesday the Italian said: "In a democratic country with freedom of speech, everyone is allowed to express their opinion.

"It's not up to me to say whether the things he says are correct, wrong or just stupid. The truth is that Romario talks a lot. A lot. It's his right."

Despite the criticism he has faced, Ancelotti feels Brazil are on the right track - and who is to tell him otherwise when you look at his track record?

"I really like what we're doing," he said.

You would have thought that would have been enough to let it lie for the time being.

But before Brazil had even kicked a ball in their next friendly against Singapore, Romario was speaking out again.

The former striker, who is the ninth-highest scorer in football history with 784 goals, doubled down on his calls for Ancelotti to be sacked.

"I talk a lot because when it comes to the national team, I have size, weight and power of speech," Romario, 60, said.

"I do not speak to gain followers, I do not speak for people to like me. I speak my mind.

"I have worn this shirt for many years and I am pretty sure I was one of the ones that helped the 'little yellow' be respected all over the world."

He said he respected Ancelotti but added he hadn't "added anything new" to the national side.

"I will say it again: resign! We will find another coach who will do a better job than you.

"And I'm saying this to your face, not through a message, including to the president of the [Brazilian Football Confederation], who is long overdue to fire you."

Brazil faced Singapore in their final match of 2026 on Tuesday and won 7-0.

Real Madrid forward Vinicius Junior, who has come under scrutiny of his own so far this season, scored a hat-trick within the opening 21 minutes while Bournemouth winger Rayan and Chelsea's Estevao were also on the scoresheet.

That result that may bring a pause to proceedings in this war of words for now.

However, if this past seven days has proved anything, it is that this saga is likely far from over.

#826. Where Hunger Games’ Jena Malone Believes Johanna Mason Is Now

Ahead of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping premiere, Jena Malone, who played Johanna Mason in the original series, shared where her character is now in an exclusive E! News interview.

Jena Malone thinks her Hunger Games character is still making them pay for it.

Over 10 years after The Hunger Games: Mockingjay—Part 2 hit theaters, Malone, who played District 7 victor Johanna Mason, revealed her hopes for where she ended up after the Panem revolution.

“I would love her to be like deep in the forest,” Malone told E! News in an exclusive interview at The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping premiere in New York Nov. 16. “Training women to do somatic warrior, like healing exercises to sort of exercise their grief.”

Given her character’s fierce personality, the Saved alum admitted that Johanna would likely “have her own army basically.”

But as she’s looking ahead at Johanna’s journey, the film franchise itself is winding the clock back with the new film, set 25 years before fans met Malone’s character.

For the actress, it was “really lovely” to reunite with former costars like Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson, Woody Harrelson, Elizabeth Banks and Willow Shields at the Sunrise on the Reaping premiere.

“It’s kind of like a homecoming,” she mused. “I feel like you get to see long lost friends. The fanbase, I feel like their enthusiasm never changes.”

And considering the upcoming film will follow a young Haymitch Abernathy—with Joseph Zada taking over the role from Harrelson—during the 50th Hunger Games, Malone considered that an origin story for her character may feature another fan favorite: District 4 victor Finnick Odair, who was played by Sam Claflin.

“It would have to be Johanna and Finnick,” she posited. “‘Cause they were in a similar game.”

Nevertheless, Malone is admittedly more interested in the reconstruction of Panem after the revolution.

“What happened to the Capitol after?” Malone considered. “I’m interested. I love when governments get overthrown, but I’m also wildly fascinated with what comes next. How do we rebuild?”

Zada, for his part, might know what lies ahead for his character Haymitch after the upcoming prequel—which hits theaters Nov. 20—but he shared he is at a loss for words after going through his own experience alongside McKenna Grace, Whitney Peak, Jesse Plemons and more.

“I don’t know how to feel,” he told E! News in a separate interview. “It feels so full circle.”

He emphasized, “I’m just so proud—I could cry right now.”

As a lifelong Hunger Games fan, Grace similarly joked that she’s been asking herself, ‘Real or Not Real?’ since scoring her dream job as Maysilee Donner.

“It’s very strange to be here and to be part of this in any regard,” she told E! on the red carpet. “It does not feel real. This is constantly like a dream I’ll wake up from. I feel so thankful.”

The actress behind Maysilee Donner was a vision of the Quarter Quell arena in this ALmée Couture dress at the U.K. premiere.

Haymitch Abernathy, is that you? The viewers will definitely remember this Gucci ensemble.

Effie Trinket would be proud of this all-pink Robert Wun look.

All's fair for the woman behind Drusilla Sickle as she walked the red carpet in a Simone Rocha gown.

The Friday Night Lights alum, who plays Plutarch Heavensbee, was ready for his close-up.

You'll love the Chanel look the Gossip Girl actress, who plays Lenore Dove, like all-fire.

The odds were ever in the Oscar winner's favor, trading Caesar Flickerman’s flashy get-up for a more classic suit.

Snow always lands on top. Just ask the actor—the third to play a version of the Hunger Games villain—at the U.K. premiere.

#825. Millwall open disciplinary proceedings against Baker

Baker featured in five Premier League games for Brighton in the 2023-24 season

Millwall are undertaking disciplinary proceedings against forward Benicio Baker following social media posts critical of senior figures at the club, BBC Sport understands.

The 22-year-old winger has played only for the Lions' under-21 side since joining from Brighton in February 2025 on a long-term deal.

BBC Sport understands the proceedings relate to a number of off-field matters, including social media activity.

Posts attributed to Baker's account, which has since been deactivated on Instagram but has been widely republished, appeared critical of senior figures at Millwall and suggested he "can't even train with the (under) 21s".

It is understood Baker was initially unavailable because of injury, but he is now the subject of disciplinary proceedings which, in the most serious circumstances, could lead to the cancellation of his contract.

Baker is also understood to be exploring options away from Millwall.

At the height of his career, Baker made six first-team appearances for Brighton under former manager Roberto de Zerbi, including in the Premier League.

The England Under-20 international also spent time in the academy systems at West Ham and Porto before making 14 senior appearances on loan as Port Vale finished second in League Two in 2024.

While at West Ham, before joining Porto, he was linked with moves to overseas clubs including Barcelona, Paris St-Germain and Benfica.

Millwall have declined to comment, while representatives for Baker have been contacted.

#824. Astronomers discover hidden alien planet in James Webb images

The Milky Way is believed to contain billions of planets beyond our solar system. These distant worlds, known as exoplanets, offer astronomers an opportunity to explore other planetary systems, identify potentially habitable environments, and perhaps eventually discover evidence of life elsewhere in the universe.

Finding these planets is one challenge. Actually seeing them is another. Most exoplanets orbit stars that shine so brightly that the planets become nearly impossible to distinguish from the surrounding glare. Even the most advanced space telescopes struggle to separate the faint light of a distant planet from the overwhelming brightness of its host star.

Now, researchers have developed a powerful new method for removing that starlight from telescope images, revealing planets that were previously hidden. The technique uses a sophisticated computer simulation of the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and has already exposed an exoplanet that was concealed in existing observations. In tests involving known planets, it achieved two to 15 times greater detection sensitivity than conventional approaches.

A Digital Twin of James Webb Reveals Hidden Planets

The breakthrough centers on a virtual replica of Webb's Near Infrared Camera (NIRCam), an instrument designed to observe the universe in infrared light. By recreating how the camera operates, researchers can identify and correct tiny imperfections that interfere with its observations.

The virtual model, often called a "digital twin," allows scientists to simulate the telescope's behavior and determine how starlight spreads through its optical system. Once they understand the patterns produced by the star, they can digitally subtract much of that glare, making faint planets easier to detect.

"Directly imaging exoplanets is incredibly challenging because even the tiniest imperfections in a telescope can make it difficult to separate the faint light of a planet from the overwhelming glare of its star," explains Caltech's Katie Bouman, professor of computing and mathematical sciences, electrical engineering and astronomy, a Rosenberg Scholar, and a Heritage Medical Research Institute Investigator, who is a co-author of a Nature paper about the new method published online November 4.

"What's exciting is that we're showing how computation can help overcome limitations of the telescope itself," Bouman continues. "By combining a physical model of the instrument with optimization techniques from machine learning, we have been able to remove starlight much more precisely, making it easier to detect faint exoplanets and even reveal one that was previously hidden in the JWST data."

How Scientists Make Blinding Starlight Disappear

The researchers named their approach Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets (FLIP). Rather than relying entirely on improvements to telescope hardware, the system uses advanced computation to correct problems in images that have already been collected.

To develop FLIP, the team created a detailed physical model of Webb's infrared camera. They then used computational techniques to examine millions of possible imperfections, subtle changes, and other unknown factors that could influence the telescope's observations.

These small variations matter because even an extremely slight distortion can alter how a star appears in an image. When astronomers attempt to remove the star's light, any remaining glare can overwhelm the much dimmer signal from a nearby planet.

By accounting for these effects, FLIP produces a highly precise model of the star's appearance. Researchers can then subtract that modeled starlight from the original observations, allowing previously obscured objects to become visible.

"This is the first time that we have demonstrated that these little imperfections or instabilities are not a limiting factor in the kinds of planets we can image," says lead author Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez, a graduate student at Northwestern University in the lab of astronomer Jason Wang, who is also a co-author of the paper. "As you go through this iterative process of trying to find what the telescope actually is doing during observations, you basically see the glare of the star disappearing in very bizarre ways. It gets dimmer and very deformed until at the end you get a pretty clean image and, if you're lucky, there's a blob there, which is a glowing planet."

A Failed Experiment Led to a Major Breakthrough

The idea behind FLIP began taking shape when Ferrer-Chavez was an undergraduate student at the Autonomous University of Yucatán in Mexico. He had already participated in a Summer Undergraduate Research Fellowship project with Wang, who was then a 51 Pegasi b Postdoctoral Fellow (named after the first exoplanet discovered orbiting a Sun-like star) in the laboratory of Dimitri Mawet.

Mawet is the David Morrisroe Professor of Astronomy at Caltech and a senior research scientist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, which is managed by Caltech. He also serves as director of instrumentation for the Caltech Optical Observatories.

At the time, Ferrer-Chavez was looking for additional opportunities to pursue research. Meanwhile, Wang had been discussing a potential collaboration with Bouman that would combine her expertise in computational imaging with his knowledge of astronomical instruments. Their shared goal was to improve the ability of telescopes to directly image exoplanets.

The two researchers brought Ferrer-Chavez into the project and began mentoring him. However, the initial effort did not produce the results they had hoped for.

"Rodrigo's senior thesis was an exploration of possible approaches, none of which ended up being what we did for this paper, but it helped rule out what not to do and also helped us understand the problem better," Wang says. "I believe our recent success was only possible because we did that exercise first."

Ferrer-Chavez originally attempted to train machine learning models to predict the patterns of starlight appearing in telescope data. That strategy proved unsuccessful, prompting the team to rethink how the technology could be used.

Instead of asking artificial intelligence to predict what the glare should look like, they turned to computational tools developed for machine learning to perform detailed physical calculations.

These methods allowed the researchers to adjust millions of variables, much like turning an enormous collection of control knobs. Each adjustment helped refine their simulation of the telescope until it more closely reproduced the actual observations. Performing this many calculations manually would be impractical.

The resulting approach combines the physical laws governing light and telescope optics with the computational power of modern optimization methods. Rather than simply guessing what should be removed from an image, FLIP uses a model of how the telescope produces that image in the first place.

James Webb's Archives May Contain More Hidden Worlds

One of the most exciting possibilities is that astronomers may not need new telescope observations to benefit from the discovery.

Webb has already collected enormous amounts of astronomical data, including images of stars that could harbor planets too faint to detect using earlier analysis methods. FLIP offers a way to revisit these observations and search for objects that were overlooked.

"We now have a tool that lets us discover and study planets that we were not able to 'see' before, even if that planet was already in an image in the JWST archive," Ferrer-Chavez explains. "We can try to find planets that may have been missed there, and also planets that perhaps we tried to image, but we could not actually detect at the time."

This means some planets that were previously considered beyond the reach of direct imaging could potentially be identified without sending another telescope into space.

It also changes how astronomers can think about existing observations. An image that appears to contain nothing but a brilliant star may hold additional information about planets hidden beneath its glare.

Pushing Telescopes Beyond Their Physical Limits

Astronomers have spent decades developing technology to reduce the overwhelming brightness of stars. One important tool is a coronagraph, an instrument designed to block starlight so that faint objects nearby can be observed more clearly.

For example, NASA's recently launched Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope carries a Coronagraph Instrument developed by researchers at Caltech, JPL, and IPAC (a science and data center for astronomy at Caltech). The instrument is specifically designed to suppress starlight and improve the direct imaging of exoplanets.

But even exceptionally precise telescope hardware has unavoidable limitations. Wang explains that physical instruments alone cannot match the level of correction achieved by FLIP when processing the images.

"The James Webb Space Telescope, which we demonstrated on, is optically stable to the nanometer level, which just sounds pretty awesome, but that's still limiting," he says. "We're excited because this technique is not limited specifically to JWST. Because of some very specific design, this technique could be used on any telescope."

A nanometer is one billionth of a meter, meaning Webb's optical system maintains extraordinary precision. Yet even disturbances on this incredibly small scale can interfere with the detection of planets next to bright stars.

FLIP offers a different way around that problem. Instead of requiring the telescope itself to eliminate every tiny imperfection, the technique mathematically accounts for those effects after the observations have been made.

The researchers now intend to refine FLIP and investigate how it could work with additional instruments, including the Roman Space Telescope and telescopes operating from Earth's surface.

A Powerful New Tool in the Search for Another Earth

The implications may extend well beyond today's observatories. The researchers believe their approach could help shape future space missions, particularly those designed to search for planets resembling Earth.

One major possibility is NASA's proposed Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO). The mission is intended to become the first telescope specifically designed to search for evidence of life on planets orbiting other stars.

A central objective would be to photograph Earth-like planets within the habitable zones of stars similar to our Sun. A habitable zone is the range of distances around a star where temperatures could allow liquid water to exist on a planet's surface, assuming suitable atmospheric conditions.

But the technical challenge is enormous. An Earth-like planet orbiting a Sun-like star can be approximately 10 billion times fainter than the star itself, making the planet extraordinarily difficult to distinguish from the surrounding light.

"The goal of HWO is to find Earth-like planets and the habitable zones of Sun-like stars through a direct imaging method," Ferrer-Chavez says. "The engineering challenge of trying to image something that is around 10 billion times fainter than something right next to it is a brutal -- not just to clean the image but to build a telescope that can take that image."

FLIP could make that challenge more manageable. If astronomers can digitally remove more unwanted starlight after capturing an image, future telescope designs may not need to overcome every source of optical instability through hardware alone.

The approach could therefore give engineers greater flexibility while allowing astronomers to extract more information from the light their instruments collect.

"I feel we just unlocked a new frontier," Wang says. "We've now gone beyond the telescope stability limit for the first time with this new technique, and this new paradigm, I think, can be applied to every instrument that's trying to image exoplanets."

Bringing the Search for Alien Life Into Focus

For Bouman, the long-term ambition is much larger than simply finding more distant planets. Astronomers ultimately hope to obtain direct images of worlds resembling Earth and examine them for possible signs of life.

Reaching that goal will require major advances in telescope engineering, astronomical instruments, and image processing. But the new research demonstrates that some of the most important improvements may come from better ways of interpreting data rather than building increasingly precise hardware.

"There's still a long way to go, but this work shows how much more is possible when we combine advances in telescope technology with computational imaging," Bouman says. "Sometimes, the key to seeing something new isn't just building a better instrument but finding a better way to make sense of the light it collects."

The findings were published in Nature in a paper titled "Imaging exoplanets below the telescope stability limit." Additional co-authors include William T. Freeman and Brandon Y. Feng of MIT, along with Laurent Pueyo and Marshall D. Perrin of the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore.

The research received support from the Space Telescope Science Institute, the Sloan Foundation, an Amazon AI4Science Discovery Award, and the National Science Foundation.

#823. Why always him? The rise and fall of Balotelli

Why always him? The rise and fall of Balotelli

Perhaps better known for off-field antics than his undeniable - yet arguably wasted - talent with the ball at his feet, the Italian has always attracted headlines.

Fifteen years have passed since his famous 'Why always me?' Manchester derby T-shirt celebration, which came just days after a firework was set off in his own bathroom, causing a house fire.

The 36-year-old is still playing, now in the United Arab Emirates first division with Al-Ittifaq alongside his biological brother, Enock Barwuah.

Here, BBC Sport looks at a career that has included 13 clubs, six countries - and an assist for arguably the most famous goal in Premier League history.

Typical of his unconventional footballing life, Balotelli's career did not begin in an elite club's academy.

Instead, by his mid-teens he was turning out for Italian third-tier side Lumezzane, close to the family home in Concesio.

A trial at Barcelona did not lead to a long-term stay, and instead he was picked up by Inter Milan in 2006.

It was at Inter that Balotelli first came across his great mentor - Roberto Mancini.

The relationship between the two has been likened to that of a father and son. Under the Italian coach's tutelage, Balotelli flourished.

Aged 17, Balotelli helped Inter win the 2007-08 Serie A title and reach the Coppa Italia final, memorably scoring twice against Juventus to send his side into the semi-finals.

Life changed for Balotelli with the arrival of Jose Mourinho in the weeks after that campaign ended.

There would be disagreements, disciplinary action and accusations that Balotelli's attitude was not up to scratch. Mourinho said Balotelli was "unmanageable" and described one performance as "close to a zero rating".

The relationship with Mourinho was fractious - a rare occasion when the Special One was confounded by a player.

Balotelli still won three Serie A titles and one Champions League with Inter, but his reputation as a supposed loose cannon was already beginning to overshadow his feats as a player.

Balotelli played for Mancini at Inter and Manchester City - and was briefly recalled for Italy by his old boss in 2018

Logic dictated that Balotelli's next step should be to reunite with mentor Mancini. That happened in August 2010 when the 20-year-old joined Manchester City.

Mancini set out to show that the unpredictable ways of Balotelli could be harnessed for the team's good, aiming to get more out of him than Mourinho could.

A hardline stance on discipline often appeared to soften when Mancini dealt with Balotelli, who by spring 2011 had garnered a reputation in England as a fantastic footballer who could not stay away from controversy.

Having already been sent off twice for City and been involved in a car crash - not in his famous camouflage Bentley but an Audi R8 - the striker threw a dart at a youth-team player, an act that showed a level of immaturity.

After helping City to win the FA Cup in 2011, ending their 35-year major trophy drought, Balotelli came under scrutiny after attempting a backheel trick shot when through on goal during a pre-season friendly against LA Galaxy.

Mancini swiftly hooked him, later questioning his mentality by saying: "If you are serious, you can play 90 minutes. If not, you can come and sit by me on the bench."

Sometimes the audacity paid off - like the famous shoulder goal and subsequent nonchalant celebration against Norwich.

In October 2011, emergency services attended his Cheshire home to deal with a firework lit in his bathroom. Balotelli said a friend had been responsible.

BBC Sport reported at the time that four firefighters used two hose reel water jets to douse the flames, with a large fan deployed to clear smoke.

Mario Balotelli scored 30 goals in 80 games for Manchester City

Days later he was in the spotlight for the right reasons as he scored City's opener in a 6-1 win over Manchester United, celebrating with the 'Why always me?' T-shirt.

There were other stories - that he had given a homeless person Â£1,000, that he had turned up to a young boy's school to confront the headmaster about the child being bullied, that he drove around Manchester handing out presents while dressed as Santa.

True? Perhaps only Balotelli knows and he has often denied such rumours. But such was his reputation at the time that the stories became plausible.

A chant City fans coined made reference to his ironic allergy to grass - which kept him out of a Europa League match in 2011 - and driving around Moss Side with "a wallet full of cash".

On the pitch, Balotelli was sent off against Arsenal in April 2012 in what, at the time, seemed like a season-defining moment that could end Manchester City's title bid.

But one month later he assisted Sergio Aguero's last-gasp goal against Queens Park Rangers that gave City a first Premier League title. It was his only Premier League assist that season.

Micah Richards, who was a team-mate and friend to Balotelli at City, said: "He was crazy in a good way. He was brilliant to have around the squad - a cult hero not just for the nonsense he did off the field but on it as well.

"The best thing about him is he's a lovely guy - he's not arrogant or how the papers try to perceive him, he's just a bit mad."

But did the moments of brilliance make the "nonsense" worth it?

Despite once insisting his patience with Balotelli was "limitless", Mancini ultimately had a rethink.

The final straw came in January 2013 when the pair had an argument at the training ground. Balotelli left for AC Milan later that month.

Mancini said: "He is not a bad guy, and a fantastic player, but I'm very sorry for him as he continues to lose his talent and his quality. I don't have any words for his behaviour.

"I hope for him he can understand he is in a bad way for his future."

Affection remained on both sides, but the relationship had become too fraught.

"Once upon a time, Mario did genuinely believe he was one of the best players in the world," said Nedum Onuoha, another former City team-mate.

"There are lots of stories about him from his time at City, but the one I remember is at our old training ground in Carrington when someone was talking about Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo, and Mario said he was as good as them - and he was deadly serious.

"It obviously hasn't worked out that way, but he still has done so much more with his career than most players could even dream of."

'Why always me?' - relive that Balotelli moment in huge Man City win

'Balotelli to Barnsley? Now that is one Mario story I don't believe'

Balotelli never threatened to have an international career to rival Ronaldo or Messi.

But there were still moments that linger in the memory.

He became the first black player to feature for Italy at a major tournament when he starred at Euro 2012.

And, more than that, he hit three goals to finish as the tournament's joint top scorer - with five others - as Italy lost to Spain in the final.

An abiding image is that of a shirtless Balotelli flexing his muscles after scoring the goal that sent the Azzurri to the final, with a 2-1 win against Germany.

Balotelli's celebration against Germany in the Euro 2012 semi-finals became an iconic image of the tournament

Yet that tournament proved to be the peak of Balotelli's international career.

Italy's national team took a downward turn, and so too did his club career. By 2015, Balotelli had more or less became an Azzurri afterthought.

While Balotelli enjoyed some big moments in an Italy shirt, he did not always feel the love reciprocated from his country of birth.

Before Euro 2012 he threatened to leave the pitch if he was subjected to racist abuse and spoke openly about the vitriol he suffered while playing for Inter.

In fact, racist abuse has followed Balotelli throughout his career and he has commendably refused to tolerate it.

Born Mario Barwuah in Palermo to Ghanaian parents, Balotelli was placed into foster care aged three.

Initially, he stayed with his foster parents - Silvia and Francesco Balotelli - in Brescia during the week, then returned to his biological parents at weekends. He was eventually fostered on a full-time basis and took on the Balotelli surname.

Balotelli identifies with both parts of his heritage - Ghana and Italy - and he struggled to reconcile his love for a nation with the people who aimed verbal abuse his way.

The good times were all too brief: 36 caps and 14 goals has been his tally since 2018. He wanted more and has often made it known.

Onuoha said: "Playing for his country was always so important to him and that's another really positive thing about him, that he had that drive and ambition."

Mancini told AC Milan that Balotelli could become one of the world's best while in Serie A.

A glut of goals followed the striker's return to the San Siro in January 2013, before a surprising move back to the Premier League followed 18 months later.

Liverpool had been impressed, but Balotelli's spell on Merseyside would prove forgettable for all. One goal in 16 Premier League games under Brendan Rodgers was not what was expected from the Â£16m buy.

The failed transfer sparked a loan move back to Milan, where injuries hampered his progress. When it was time for Balotelli to return to Merseyside, Jurgen Klopp had arrived and said the striker would not be part of his Liverpool plans.

Balotelli later called the move to Anfield "the worst mistake of my life".

Steven Gerrard and Mario Balotelli were briefly Liverpool team-mates - but it didn't work out at Anfield for the Italian

Was it that Liverpool move that sent Balotelli's career spiralling into freefall?

Spells in Nice, Marseille, Brescia and Monza followed - each to varying degrees of success but never with a feeling of stability.

Then came Turkish club Adana Demirspor, Swiss outfit Sion and Italian side Genoa. He spent no more than one season at a time with any of these clubs, although he did return to Demirspor for a second stint.

And so to the present day, with Balotelli aged 36 and plying his trade in the UAE.

It is easy to wonder what might have been had Balotelli stayed in Manchester, had he managed to settle enough to entirely fulfil his potential.

But, after so much media attention and a career that has spanned more continents and leagues than most, it is perhaps also understandable that Balotelli has settled on fulfilment through simply playing the game he loves with his brother.

"Playing with a family member like he is will give him that happiness," said Onuoha.

"And yes, it is not Serie A, La Liga or the Premier League, but Mario is on a field sharing it with his brother - for him that will mean everything.

"At this point there aren't many people that would hold much against him. I think when he was younger, some people would.

"But now I think it is more a case of almost allowing him this happiness, and enjoying seeing him finish off the last days of his career in a place that makes him happy.

"So many people end their careers on a sour note, but for him he is going to be ending it doing exactly what he wants to do."

#822. A radical theory says the universe is twice as old as we thought

A radical alternative to the standard picture of the cosmos is gaining attention after researchers at the University of Ottawa reported that it successfully matched several important astronomical observations. The model suggests that the Universe could be 26.7 billion years old, nearly twice the widely accepted age of 13.8 billion years, and that neither dark matter nor dark energy is needed to explain its behavior.

If further research supports these findings, the theory could offer a very different explanation for how the Universe evolved. It may also help resolve one of modern astronomy's most puzzling discoveries: the existence of surprisingly large and mature galaxies at a time when the conventional model suggests they should barely have begun forming.

Throughout 2025 and 2026, Rajendra Gupta, an adjunct professor in the University of Ottawa's Department of Physics, and postdoctoral researcher Dr. Nikolaos Samaras evaluated an alternative cosmological framework known as CCC+TL against several major astronomical observations.

The name stands for “covarying coupling constants plus tired light.” Rather than relying on dark matter and dark energy, the model proposes that some of the effects attributed to these mysterious components could result from changes over time in fundamental physical constants. These constants help determine how particles and forces interact.

For decades, astronomers have searched for direct evidence of dark matter and dark energy. Dark matter is thought to provide additional gravity that helps explain how galaxies move and how large cosmic structures hold together. Dark energy is the name given to whatever is causing the expansion of the Universe to accelerate. Although extensive observations support their gravitational and cosmological effects, neither component has been directly identified.

The prevailing cosmological framework, called ΛCDM, incorporates both. Despite its success in explaining a wide range of observations, it faces questions raised by the discovery of unexpectedly developed galaxies in the early Universe.

“Most emerging models explain only a limited set of observations,” Professor Gupta says. “A new model must not conflict with the pillars of cosmology and astrophysics, and our findings meet that challenge, including the yet-to-be-published Cosmic Microwave Background challenge.”

Testing such a fundamentally different theory requires more than adjusting the standard model. CCC+TL modifies the Einstein and Friedmann equations, which describe gravity and how the Universe expands. As a result, Gupta and Samaras had to develop equations and computer programs specifically adapted to their model for each test.

The researchers report that CCC+TL produced results consistent with several major astronomical measurements. One important test involved the light elements created shortly after the Big Bang, including hydrogen and helium. The alternative model predicted abundances that matched those calculated using the standard cosmological framework.

It also agreed with cosmic chronometer measurements, which allow astronomers to reconstruct the history of cosmic expansion by comparing the ages of galaxies at different distances. These measurements provide an independent way to examine how the expansion rate has changed over billions of years.

Another significant test focused on the motion of galaxies. In a recent study published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, the researchers examined all 175 galaxies in the SPARC database. They found that their model could reproduce the observed rotation curves without invoking dark matter.

Rotation curves describe how quickly stars and gas orbit at different distances from the centers of galaxies. Under conventional gravity, the visible matter alone generally cannot explain these motions, which is one of the major reasons scientists believe dark matter exists.

The team also investigated time dilation in observations of supernovae. Time dilation refers to the apparent stretching of events over time when viewed across vast cosmic distances. Their analysis offered additional support for CCC+TL, although the research paper remains under review.

The researchers also examined the Bullet Cluster, a famous system of colliding galaxy clusters that provides some of the strongest observational evidence for dark matter.

In this system, most of the ordinary matter is concentrated in extremely hot gas that emits X-rays. However, observations show that much of the gravitational effect is associated with the galaxies rather than the gas. The standard explanation is that invisible dark matter passed through the collision along with the galaxies.

Under CCC+TL, the additional gravitational effect predicted by the model also follows the galaxies instead of the hot gas, but without requiring dark matter. The researchers emphasize that this result is only an initial proof of concept and that more detailed investigations are necessary.

“Observations attributed to dark matter and dark energy likely originate from covarying coupling constants,” adds Professor Gupta, who examines this possibility further in a separate paper exploring the origin of dark matter and dark energy.

Perhaps the most intriguing implication of the model involves the earliest galaxies ever observed.

Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope have discovered galaxies that appear surprisingly massive and mature for their early place in cosmic history. Their existence has prompted questions about how quickly stars and galaxies could have formed after the Big Bang.

CCC+TL offers a possible answer by giving the early Universe substantially more time to develop.

In the standard cosmological model, the Universe was approximately 300 million years old during the period known as cosmic dawn, when the first generations of stars and galaxies were emerging. At the same observed redshift, however, CCC+TL would place the Universe's age at roughly 4.6 billion years.

Redshift measures how much light from a distant object has shifted toward longer, redder wavelengths. Astronomers use it to study distant galaxies and investigate earlier stages of cosmic history.

Under the alternative model, galaxies observed at extremely high redshifts would have had billions of additional years to grow. The researchers calculate that early galaxies would be approximately 12 times larger in both size and mass than predicted by standard cosmology, according to findings published in Galaxies 13, 115.

“Impossible early galaxies become predictable galaxies,” Professor Gupta explains. “We predict that galaxies exist well beyond the distances the James Webb Space Telescope has reached.”

Upcoming observations could provide an important opportunity to investigate this prediction.

The James Webb Space Telescope's GLIMPSE program aims to search for extremely distant galaxies, potentially reaching redshifts greater than 50. These observations would probe an exceptionally early period in the Universe's history under the standard cosmological framework.

According to conventional models, there may not have been enough time for large galaxies to assemble at such extreme redshifts. The CCC+TL model does not impose the same restriction because its cosmic timeline allows substantially more time for galaxies to develop.

Finding galaxies at these distances could therefore provide another important way to compare the competing explanations. However, such discoveries would not, by themselves, establish that the alternative model is correct.

Although the researchers report encouraging results across several major cosmological tests, CCC+TL remains an unconventional proposal that requires further independent examination. The standard cosmological model continues to explain a broad range of astronomical observations, and any replacement must ultimately demonstrate comparable or greater success.

For Gupta, the latest findings provide a reason to continue investigating the possibility that the Universe operates differently than scientists currently assume.

“The success should encourage astronomers to take the new model seriously. It is challenging to understand and apply, but we believe it extends the physics of the Universe beyond ΛCDM limits,” concludes Professor Gupta.

Materials provided by University of Ottawa. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#820. Mariah Carey, Nick Cannon's Twins Make Rare Comments About Siblings

Nick Cannon as well as his and Mariah Carey’s kids Moroccan and Monroe revealed what led to his divorce from the “Honey” singer in the official trailer for Netflix’s Raising the Cannons.

Nick Cannon didn’t give his all during his and Mariah Carey’s 8-year marriage.

The Wild ‘n Out star recently revealed what led to his 2016 divorce from the Grammy winner in the trailer for his upcoming Netflix docuseries Raising the Cannons, out Dec. 18, revealing it was his own actions that ultimately led to the split.

As Nick put it in the trailer which was released Nov. 17, “My ego drove me away from Mariah.”

Meanwhile, the pair’s 15-year-old twins Moroccan and Monroe appeared to agree as they shared rare insight into their parents’ breakup, as well.

For Monroe, it’s her father’s blended family—Nick is dad to 10 other children with five separate women—that has kept the couple from rekindling their romance.

“If you didn't have all these kids,” she said during a car ride with Nick, “you would have been back together.”

Echoing his sister, Moroccan added in a later confessional, “This lifestyle, I don't think it's sustainable in any way.”

Nevertheless, Nick, 46, recently revealed that he and Mariah, 57, have the best dynamic yet nearly 10 years after their divorce.

“We talk almost every day or every other day, specifically just about the kids,” Nick told Us Weekly in an interview published in September. “We were laughing about [reports we’re not close]. I was like, ‘Who is telling people that?’”

After all, the Love Don’t Cost a Thing actor emphasized that his and Mariah’s split “wasn’t messy,” and that they "were able to move on and be the best parents we can.”

And while these days Nick engages in consensual nonmognaomy in his love life, he made it clear that wasn’t the case during his and Mariah’s marriage.

“I was married for seven-plus years, and my wife was the only person I was monogamous with because I didn’t want to f--k it up,” he admitted. “I was like, 'This is Mariah Carey. I’m not messing this up!’”

Still, Nick wouldn’t change his choice to expand his family.

“But I have an abundance of love, and I want to be the best provider and partner,” he added. “I have the means to—not even speaking financially—be a helpmate to people and I think that’s the root of it.”

Keep reading for a closer look at Nick’s family tree…

Children No. 1 and 2: Moroccan Cannon and Monroe Cannon

Mariah Carey gave birth to her and Nick's twins on April 30, 2011. The two announced their split in 2015 after six years of marriage and finalized their divorce a year later.

Beauty queen Brittany Bell gave birth to her and Nick's first child together, a boy, on Feb. 21, 2017.

Brittany and Nick welcomed their second baby together, a girl, in December 2020.

DJ Abby De La Rosa gave birth to her and Nick's twin boys on June 14, 2021.

Model Alyssa Scott welcomed a baby boy with Nick on June 23, 2021.

However, just five months after the arrival of their son, Nick shared the devastating news that Zen had passed away from brain cancer. "Alyssa was just the strongest woman I have ever seen," he said on the Dec. 7 episode of The Nick Cannon Show. "Never had an argument, never was angry. She was emotional when she needed to be but was always the best mom and continues to be the best mom possible. So I've got to say thank you to my entire family but specifically to Alyssa."

"You never know what someone is going through," he added. "Hug your family. Kiss somebody. Tell them you love them."

Model Bre Tiesi welcomed her first child with Nick on June 28, 2022. The baby boy weighed 8 pounds and 10 ounces at birth.

"I did it. An all natural unmedicated home birth," Bre shared in a July 2022 Instagram post. "This was the most humbling / limit pushing yet awakening and completely empowering experience. I can't thank my team enough for delivering my son safely."

Nick and model LaNisha Cole welcomed a daughter on Sept. 14, 2022.

Brittany gave birth to her third child with Nick on Sept. 23, 2022.

Abby gave birth to a baby girl, her third child with Nick, in November 2022.

Alyssa gave birth to her and Nick's daughter on Dec. 14, 2022.

The model shared an Instagram video showing the Wild 'n Out star helping to deliver their baby. "Our lives are forever changed," she wrote. "Zen is in every breath I take. I know his spirit was with us in the room that morning. I know he is watching down on us. He shows me signs everyday. I will hold onto this memory forever."

She continued, "I will remember the sound of Nicks voice saying 'it's a girl' and the look of everything we've been through flash across his face. I will remember the sound of her crying out with her first breath and feeling her heartbeat against mine. My sweet girl, I got my surprise!! We love you Halo Marie Cannon!"

#819. Euclid space telescope discovers its 1st comet | Space photo of the day for Nov. 16, 2026

Join The Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

The new observatory managed to catch this comet whirling between the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Euclid space telescope has discovered its first comet, called comet C/2026 S1, or comet Euclid for short.

The Euclid mission, a European Space Agency mission that launched in 2023 with contributions from NASA, spotted this previously undetected comet approximately 807 million miles (1.3 billion kilometers) away in observations captured between Sept. 16 and 24.

"I was excited to see my software flag a 'streak' smeared across several images – the result of a fast-moving object. By predicting its position I could identify it in other images, in total finding it in five image sets. Further inspection revealed that it had a fuzzy cloud around it, indicative of an active object like a comet that is shedding dust and gas," Mikko Pöntinen, a scientist at the University of Helsinki who made the initial discovery with a Solar System Objects Science Working Group within the Euclid Consortium, said in a statement.

Following these observations, the team diligently checked current records of comets to ensure that this was, in fact, something new to us.

Euclid is a mission designed to capture long, slow observations of deep space and distant galaxies and collect data to help scientists better unravel the mysteries of dark energy and dark matter. It was in not explicitly designed in any way to capture imagery of fast-moving comet hurtling through our solar system. But still, the space telescoped managed to catch this comet whirling between the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn.

This finding shows that Euclid can be used for more than it was intended, and that in the future scientists could use it to intentionally target other comets in the far reaches of our solar neighborhood. These kinds of observations can also help researchers to identify "noise" like comet trails in Euclid's field of view.

Chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. When not writing, editing or filming something space-y, Gohd is writing music and performing as Foxanne, even launching a song to space in 2021 with Inspiration4. #817. Julia Garner Reunites With Anna Delvey After Inventing Anna Role

Four years after Julia Garner played disgraced criminal socialite Anna Delvey in Netflix’s Inventing Anna, the actress and her muse reunited at a screening for The Altruists in New York.

VIP is always better, but this reunion is simply the best.

Four years after Julia Garner’s Emmy-winning portrayal of Anna Delvey in Inventing Anna, the actress reunited with the fake socialite at a fan screening for The Altruists.

At the Nov. 16 event for the Netflix series—which chronicles the rise and fall of the now-incarcerated FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried and exec Caroline Ellison—Garner and Delvey shared a warm moment together on the red carpetat the Paris Theater in New York. In fact, the convicted con artist (real name Anna Sorokin) even joined in on the question and answer segment with the Ozark alum and Altruists creator Graham Moore on stage.

Delvey, for her part, was looking as chic as ever, sporting a black skirt suit with a fitted blazer, tights and her blonde hair styled into a swoopy lob. Of course, the 35-year-old also sported a required accessory with her ankle monitor wrapped around her left leg. (Delvey is currently under a flexible house arrest from the Immigration and Customs Enforcement following her 2021 release from prison.)

Garner, for her part, matched Delvey’s color palette in a halter knee-length dress with an attached long-sleeved cover.

And while it’s been years since Garner portrayed Delvey on screen in the Netflix series, the duo’s history dates back even further to when Garner visited Delvey during her nearly four-year prison sentence following her conviction of grand larceny.

“She was very nice,” Delvey said of Garner’s visit during a 2022 appearance on the Forbidden Fruits podcast. “She came to see me and she’s a very sweet girl.”

Nevertheless, Delvey had one problem with Garner’s take on her: her iconic accent.

“It's just so weird,” she admitted, “because the way you hear yourself—like your voice is just completely different when you hear yourself on TV.”

Still, Delvey defended Garner’s artistic liberties.

“She was portraying me from like, 2015, 2016, 2017,” the Dancing with the Stars alum explained. “So now I've spent the past four years just in the States. I was surrounded by Americans so maybe my accent was different.”

To Delvey, her voice has evolved even since her prison sentence.

#816. After 40 years, CERN finds evidence of a one-in-10-billion particle decay

After more than 40 years of searching, physicists at CERN have reached a major milestone in their hunt for one of the rarest known particle decays. Researchers working with the LHCb experiment have detected evidence of a process expected to occur only once in approximately 10 billion beauty particle decays.

The finding, announced during a seminar at CERN, marks the first time a single experiment has produced sufficient evidence for this extraordinarily rare event. Beyond its rarity, the decay is particularly valuable because it could help scientists investigate particles that are too massive to be created directly in the Large Hadron Collider.

At the center of the discovery is a particle called Bd, which contains a beauty quark and a down antiquark. Scientists found evidence that this particle can decay into a pair of muons (μ+μ-). Muons are similar to electrons but have greater mass. The results agree with predictions from the Standard Model, the leading theory describing fundamental particles and their interactions, and help narrow the possibilities for new particles beyond it.

Why Rare Particle Decays Could Reveal New Physics

One reason physicists are so interested in these unusual decays is that quantum effects allow other particles to influence how they occur. Even particles too heavy to be produced in the Large Hadron Collider can potentially leave subtle traces in the rates of these processes.

By measuring extremely rare decays with high precision, researchers can look for differences between experimental results and theoretical predictions. Such discrepancies could provide indirect evidence of previously unknown particles. Generally, the rarer a decay is, the more sensitive it can be to these hidden influences.

The decay known as Bd → μ+μ-belongs to a special category that physicists have long considered 'golden channels' for investigating physics beyond the Standard Model. During this process, a beauty quark and an antiquark with the opposite electric charge annihilate each other. Their energy is transformed into a muon and its antiparticle.

Scientists have previously observed a related process involving a different beauty particle, called Bs. In 2015, a joint analysis by the LHCb and CMS collaborations reported the first confirmed observation of Bs → μ+μ-, along with initial evidence for the much rarer Bd decay.

However, subsequent analyses incorporating data collected through 2018 could not confirm the earlier evidence for Bd → μ+μ-. The difference in rarity is substantial. The Bs decay occurs approximately three times per billion beauty particle decays, while the Bd process is predicted to happen about 30 times less frequently.

Upgraded CERN Detector Makes the Breakthrough Possible

A significant improvement to the LHCb experiment helped researchers overcome the enormous difficulty of detecting such a rare event.

Following a major upgrade, the experiment began collecting data in 2024 at five times the rate achieved between 2010 and 2018. The upgraded detector also became better at identifying different kinds of particles, giving researchers a clearer picture of the activity produced during collisions.

The team combined these improvements with machine learning techniques to distinguish the exceptionally rare signals from the vast number of other particle processes. Without these advances, the events scientists wanted to study would have been overwhelmed by the background.

"Physicists have been chasing this decay for more than forty years," said Marco Santimaria, who co-led the international analysis team of 19 scientists. "Extreme precision is required to pick the muons out of the overwhelming background."

Four Decades of Searching Finally Produce Strong Evidence

In particle physics, scientists use a statistical measure called standard deviations to evaluate how likely an apparent signal is to result from random fluctuations rather than a genuine physical process.

A result must reach three standard deviations to qualify as evidence of a new phenomenon. At that level, the probability of random fluctuations producing a signal at least as statistically extreme is approximately 0.3%.

Using data collected during 2024 and 2025, the LHCb researchers identified evidence of Bd → μ+μ- at a significance of 3.0 standard deviations. When they combined those measurements with earlier data gathered between 2011 and 2018, the statistical significance increased to 3.2 standard deviations, exceeding the widely accepted threshold for evidence.

The same investigation also produced the most precise measurements ever obtained for the related Bs → μ+μ-decay, providing additional information about these exceptionally uncommon processes.

Although the new findings represent a major achievement, physicists have not yet reached the threshold required to declare a confirmed observation. That milestone requires a significance of five standard deviations.

If future measurements achieve that level of certainty, Bd → μ+μ-would become the rarest beauty particle decay ever observed.

Future Large Hadron Collider Upgrades Could Uncover Hidden Particles

Researchers expect upcoming improvements to the Large Hadron Collider to make these measurements even more powerful.

The High Luminosity LHC, also known as the HiLumi LHC, is scheduled to begin operating in 2030. Another major upgrade to the LHCb experiment is planned for the middle of the following decade. Together, these developments could eventually increase the experiment's data collection rate by another factor of ten.

Collecting much larger datasets would allow physicists to detect more of these extremely rare decays and measure their properties with greater precision. That increased sensitivity could make it possible to identify subtle effects associated with particles that remain beyond the direct reach of existing accelerators.

"Seeing evidence of this rare decay is incredibly exciting, opening up new possibilities to probe beyond the direct reach of the LHC," explained Harry Cliff, LHCb's Rare Decays Convener and Analysis Co-lead.

"The future LHCb upgrade will allow us to observe many more of these decays, providing even greater sensitivity to undiscovered particles."

For physicists who have pursued this elusive signal for more than four decades, the new evidence represents a long-awaited advance. It also offers a promising way to investigate whether the known laws of particle physics are part of a much larger picture.
