#801. Senegal and Morocco lead Afcon qualifiers but Tunisia protest

Senegal were stripped of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations title by a Confederation of African Football appeals board, and are awaiting the outcome of their own appeal at the Court of Arbitration for Sport

Senegal became the first side to qualify for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations before Cameroon and Morocco were among five others to join them with two games to spare - but there was penalty drama in Tripoli.

Tunisia, who have appeared at a record 17 consecutive editions of Afcon, are at risk of missing out after a contentious 1-1 draw against Libya.

Libya's penalty equaliser just before half-time followed protest scenes lasting over five minutes as players and staff from the Carthage Eagles challenged the decision.

The video assistant referee system is not used in Afcon qualifying, and Tunisia's remonstrating with the fourth official on the touchline ultimately only served to delay the spot-kick, which Ezoo El Mariamy, the player who was adjudged to have been fouled, converted.

Drawing the game meant Tunisia's winless start in Group H continued, with the Carthage Eagles having just three points from four games.

Tunisia need a strong finish to their campaign to give themselves a chance of reaching the finals, and Nigeria are also at risk of missing out, but others have made short order of qualifying.

Led by new head coach Patrick Vieira, Senegal moved to the brink of a place at the finals by beating Sudan 4-2 on Monday, and the Teranga Lions had their passage from Group J confirmed on Tuesday when Mozambique secured a 1-0 victory away against Ethiopia.

Cameroon and Benin also progressed without kicking a ball after Comoros and Burkina Faso registered wins - with the latter result also sealing a finals spot for the victorious Stallions.

Mali and Morocco extended their perfect starts and booked their places with triumphs over Rwanda and Niger respectively.

Abdellah Ouazane was the match-winner for Morocco in an away game that was actually played in Rabat, with the 17-year-old brilliantly curling in midway through the first half to cap a fine team move.

The Atlas Lions and Senegal are still waiting for the outcome of a case at the Court of Arbitration for Sport to decide the destination of the 2025 Afcon title.

Senegal won the final 1-0 after extra time but Morocco were awarded the trophy by a Confederation of African Football appeals board which decreed the West Africans breached competition regulations by leaving the field of play in second-half stoppage time in protest at a penalty awarded against them.

Cameroon, Senegal and Benin close in on Afcon 2027 qualification

Why has Caf abandoned plans to hold Afcon every four years?

Eleven sides had the chance to join co-hosts Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda at next year's finals when the fourth round of fixtures culminated on Tuesday.

Algeria, DR Congo, Egypt and the Ivorians all could have qualified with away wins but failed to pick up three points.

Brighton forward Yankuba Minteh was on target as The Gambia came from behind to lead Ivory Coast 2-1 in Group C, but Christ Inao Oulai grabbed an equaliser deep in stoppage time after Scorpions striker Muhammed Badamosi was sent off in the 90th minute.

Egypt were held to a goalless draw in Malawi, Sierra Leone claimed a late point against the Congolese and Algeria suffered a 3-0 defeat in Togo.

Angola beat South Sudan 1-0 in Juba and would have qualified had Egypt claimed victory in the other match in Group B.

Nigeria are in danger of failing to reach Afcon for the first time since 2017 after the Super Eagles failed to beat Tanzania.

The final two rounds of qualifiers will be held in March next year, with Afcon 2027 scheduled to be held in East Africa from 19 June to 17 July.

Malawi goalkeeper George Chikooka helped deny Mohamed Salah's Egypt an early passage to the Afcon 2027 finals in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda

Seven-time Afcon winners Egypt knew victory in Lilongwe could take them to the finals but were frustrated by an inspired second-half showing from Malawi goalkeeper George Chikooka.

After Pharaohs captain Mohamed Salah had hit the outside of the post from a tight angle, Chikooka denied Trezeguet and Haissem Hassan before also making fine stops from Mohamed Hany and Ibrahim Adel in stoppage time.

Egypt move on to eight points in Group B, two points behind Angola after Miro's first-half effort secured a 1-0 victory for the Palancas Negras in Juba.

There was drama as Ivory Coast salvaged a draw in Bakau through Inao Oulai's 98th-minute goal, which denied The Gambia a third win in Group C.

The Ivorians lead the pool on 10 points, with The Gambia on seven and Ghana on six following the Black Stars' back-to-back wins over Somalia.

DR Congo appeared on track to progress from Group E as Junior Kadile gave the Leopards a half-time lead in their away tie against Sierra Leone, but Alie Conteh netted in the 94th minute for the West Africans.

And Togo moved a point behind Group I leaders Algeria after a strong first-half showing in Lome, with two goals from Thibault Klidje before Kennedy Boateng's powerful header secured a 3-0 win over the 2019 champions from North Africa.

Eric Chelle's Nigeria failed to qualify for the 2026 Fifa World Cup and now face an uphill battle to reach Afcon 2027

Nigeria's hopes of progressing suffered another blow as Eric Chelle's men drew 0-0 with Tanzania in Zanzibar.

With East Africans Tanzania already assured of a spot at the finals, as co-hosts, Nigeria are competing with Guinea-Bissau for just one qualification spot available in Group L.

And Guinea-Bissau established a three-point advantage over the Super Eagles as goals from Mama Balde and Mauro Rodrigues gave them a 2-0 home win over Madagascar.

After falling to a 3-0 defeat in Bissau in September, even maximum points in the final two rounds of qualifiers may not be enough for three-time continental champions Nigeria to reach the tournament.

In another section with just one qualifying berth, Tunisia are in trouble at the foot of Group H on three points after the 1-1 draw with Libya in Tripoli.

Anis Ben Slimane capitalised on a defensive error to fire Tunisia ahead in the third minute, but El Mariamy levelled for the hosts from 12 yards in first-half injury time.

Tunisia's players and officials vehemently protested against the decision to award a foul after El Mariamy tussled with defender Ghaith Zaalouni and collided with goalkeeper Aymen Dahmen, delaying the penalty for several minutes.

The Tunisian visitors then had their own claims for a spot-kick turned down after a similar coming together between Mohamed Belhadj Mahmoud and Libya keeper Ayman Al Tihar, with players surrounding Beninois referee Adissa Ligali and his assistants at the full-time whistle.

The Carthage Eagles had also complained about refereeing decisions in the reverse fixture on Friday with a potential equaliser ruled out following a marginal offside call, before their North African neighbours sealed a 2-0 win.

Libya are one point behind Group H leaders Uganda after the Cranes drew 1-1 away against Botswana, who are one point better off than Tunisia.

Elsewhere, South Africa returned to the top of Group D with a 2-1 win over co-hosts Kenya, Cape Verde's chances of reaching the finals were hit by a 2-0 defeat in Liberia and Gabon suffered a shock 2-0 loss at the hands of Lesotho.

Benin, Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Kenya (co-hosts), Mali, Morocco, Senegal, Tanzania (co-hosts), Uganda (co-hosts).

#800. FA wants to host Nations League finals in England

England finished top of their Nations League group

England could host the Nations League finals this season after Football Association officials registered their interest.

The semi-final and finals of the competition, due to take place in June, are held in one country.

As well as England, it is understood that Spain and France have also contacted Uefa to register their interest in hosting the final four games, including the bronze medal match, which will run between 9-13 June.

The FA, it is understood, is still discussing potential venues with some doubt over whether Wembley would be available. The only publicly announced Wembley events in June are two concerts by singer Sam Fender, although these are for after the Nations League.

Since the tournament began in 2019, England have never held the finals, with Portugal, Italy, Netherlands and Germany the hosts to date.

Generally, only nations who reach the last four of the Nations League are considered to host the latter stages.

Thomas Tuchel's team will be seeded in Friday's draw for the quarter-finals following their euphoric 3-2 victory over Spain in Madrid, which secured top place in the group.

They could face Belgium, Netherlands, Denmark or Norway in March in the next round before June's finals.

If the FA's bid is successful, it will provide the governing body with an opportunity to host a mini-tournament before Euro 2028, which will be held in England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland.

#799. Brad Pitt Teases How He's Celebrating Birthday Out of the Spotlight

Brad Pitt exclusively shared with E! News at The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth premiere Nov. 16 how he's celebrating his 63rd birthday—and it involves some quiet time away from the spotlight.

Brad Pitt is ready for an ocean of celebrations.

The Ocean’s Eleven star revealed how he plans to celebrate his upcoming 63rd birthday in December, admitting he’s looking forward to getting away from the spotlight for a moment.

“I got a little spot up north,” Pitt exclusively shared with E! News’ Will Marfuggi at the Nov. 16 Los Angeles premiere of The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth. “I just like to chill and be quiet out in the nature.”

Of course, the celebrations will be extra special as his girlfriend Ines de Ramon turns 34 on Dec. 19—just one day after his Dec. 18 birthday.

And a little bit of quiet will certainly be warranted after the whirlwind promotional schedule for The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, in which Pitt reprises his Oscar-winning role from 2019’s Once Upon a Time in… Hollywood.

“It's pretty cozy,” he shared with E! about returning to the character. “In fact, I was a little concerned ‘cause I was like, ‘What did I do in the first one?’”

Luckily, Pitt was able to rely on costars like Carla Gugino, Timothy Olyphant and Elizabeth Debicki, as well as the film’s director David Fincher. In fact, he emphasized that with the Mindhunter creator at the helm, he knew he was “in the best of hands.”

Especially after screenwriter Quentin Tarantino—who wrote and directed Once Upon a Time in… Hollywood—had a whole new vision for Cliff Booth, who in the original film served as the stunt double for Leonardo DiCaprio’s Rick Dalton.

“He’s a lot a bit of a fixer, which was a surprise to me,” Pitt admitted. “You never know what Quentin's brewing.”

And while he played a fixer in the movies, there was only one person from his list of Hollywood pals that he would truly trust to fix anything. “Oh, [George] Clooney, without a doubt,” Pitt exclaimed. “Oh yeah, no question. He's pretty savvy.”

The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is in theaters and IMAX on Nov. 25 before dropping on Netflix Dec. 23.

Though Pitt likes to take space from Hollywood, some stars have fully walked away in the glitz and glamour of the city. Keep reading to find out who has ditched Hollywood for a quieter life.

After the Mask of Zorro actor suffered a near-fatal heart attack in 2019, he moved back to his native Málago, Spain, to focus on his love of theater.

“It changed the way I look at life,” Banderas told The Times in March 2026. “Faced with death, it made me look back and realise that I am, in fact, a theater actor.”

Now, the Tony nominee—who still occasionally takes on TV and film projects—owns a theater venue and gets involved with the local community.

“I have never been so happy,” he continued. “It keeps me in touch with my roots, my neighbourhood, my people. I haven’t lost that connection over the years. Quite the opposite.”

Before landing a role in Prime Video's Every Year After, The Girl Next Door actress took a four-year break from acting, leaving L.A. to raise her two kids with husband Dion Phaneuf.

"I realized I worked all four years through our first child and it was really hard," Cuthbert confessed in June 2026 during an appearance on Today, "to separate that mom from the working person I was. So, when we had our second, I just felt like I didn't want to waste any second of it and I didn't want to be on set."

Cuthbert—best known for starring in '00s films like Old School as well as hit TV shows including 24 and Happy Endings—added, "I just felt like I needed to be at home with the kids and I enjoyed every minute."

The actress, known for her roles on hit TV dramas like Fire Country, Numb3rs and Rescue Me, shared in July 2026 that she sold her Los Angeles home after living there for 30 years to embark on her "third chapter" somewhere far away from Hollywood.

"I came here chasing a dream that I am still shocked worked out," she wrote on Instagram. "And I also got to raise babies in the sun and the mountains and enjoy this beautiful home and attend public schools ?? Pinch me I’m overwhelmed by the blessings and hope, really hope I gave enough back. LA will always be where my family is from."

The Ellen DeGeneres Show host's eponymous talk show ended in 2022 after a 19-season run amid allegations of a toxic work environment that prompted an internal investigation, multiple firings of executives and public ire.

DeGeneres returned to the spotlight for her final standup special For Your Approval, which released on Netflix in September 2024. During the lead-up to that special, she revealed she would be leaving Hollywood altogether.

"This is the last time you’re going to see me," she told a crowd during her Ellen’s Last Stand…Up tour, per SFGate. “After my Netflix special, I’m done."

DeGeneres and her wife Portia de Rossi have since moved to the Cotswolds, deciding to stay put in November 2024 after Donald Trump's reelection, the talk show host told to Richard Bacon in a July 2025 conversation at the Everyman theater in Cheltenham.

"It's absolutely beautiful," she gushed about the English countryside, per the BBC. "We're just not used to seeing this kind of beauty. The villages and the towns and the architecture—everything you see is charming and it's just a simpler way of life.

"It's clean," DeGeneres continued. "Everything here is just better—the way animals are treated, people are polite. I just love it here. We moved here in November, which was not the ideal time, but I saw snow for the first time in my life. We love it here. Portia flew her horses here, and I have chickens, and we had sheep for about two weeks."

One of the reasons the America's Next Top Model host moved to Australia? To stay on top of her ice cream brand."So I have this ice cream company, SMiZE and Dream," Banks explained on an April 2025 episode of Today with Jenna & Friends. “But we've been more what we call B2B, like on an airplane and on cruises. I’ve been going to Australia a lot because we were making a lot of our ice cream there in a big facility doing our recipes. And I just fell in love with it every time I went back and went back."Not only was she happy there, but she also knew it was a good market for her business."The three countries that eat the most ice cream?" she continued. "America, New Zealand and Australia."So, the supermodel moved to Australia with her son York (his dad is her ex Erik Asla) and boyfriend Louis Bélanger-Martin, noting, "Australia has been a dream come true for me and my family."

While it's been a minute since the Desperate Housewives star lived on Wisteria Lane, she's since found a new address IRL."I had my whole adult life here," Eva told Marie Claire in November 2024 about leaving Los Angeles. "But even before [the pandemic], it was changing. The vibe was different. And then Covid happened, and it pushed it over the edge. Whether it’s the homelessness or the taxes, not that I want to s--t on California—it just feels like this chapter in my life is done now."So for the past few years, the actress, her husband José Bastón and their son Santiago have split their time between Mexico and Spain."I’m privileged," she continued. "I get to escape and go somewhere. Most Americans aren’t so lucky. They’re going to be stuck in this dystopian country, and my anxiety and sadness is for them."However, Eva noted her move wasn't because of President Trump's re-election."I didn't leave because of the political environment," the Flamin' Hot director said on The View: Behind the Table podcast in November 2024. "I left because my work took me there since Land of Women—shooting six months in Catalonia, then four months in Mexico for Searching for Mexico, then back to Spain. Now I've been there for years. So I just don't like that it's politicized."Since moving, Eva has continued to stay busy, with recent projects including her roles in Only Murders in the Building and Alexander and the Terrible, Horrible, No Good, Very Bad Road Trip.

The actor has gone from Chicago to Spain."My wife is Spanish, and she gave me about seven years here," Richard said of Galicia native Alejandra Silva on a November 2024 episode of The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon. "And so we're going to spend some years in Madrid."He also expressed his excitement over what the move would give the couple's young sons Alexander and James."Our kids are bilingual," Richard, who also has an adult son Homer with ex Carey Lowell, added, "so they're going to flourish there."Indeed, it seems the whole family has."The truth is that you are seeing us in our momentum," The Agency: Central Intelligence star told Elle España in January 2025. "We are happier than ever."

From AM to PM, the singer is living in Paris "My husband is French, and we've been together for over seven or eight years," Milian, who is married to singer Matt Pokora, said on a November 2024 episode of The Jennifer Hudson Show. "And for the last three or four years we were commuting back and forth every six months."However, they decided to officially say au revoir to the U.S. so her kids—who include daughter Violet from her former marriage with The-Dream and sons Isaiah and Kenna from her union with Pokora—could study in France."They're all going to school in Paris," she continued. "I was like, 'What better than an opportunity than that?"And life for the family appears to be magnifique."My kids are happy there," the Dexter: Original Sin actress told E! in December 2024. "They know French. We go to the park. I have an active lifestyle that's really nice during the day. Then at night time, I do my work because I work hours ahead. It's a nice, healthy balance for me."

The Mean Girls star is tired of rumors starting about why she left Los Angeles.So, she set the record straight while looking back at her hectic work schedule and partying in the aughts. "I feel like some of [my work] got overshadowed by paparazzi and all that kind of stuff when I was younger, and that’s kind of annoying," the Parent Trap alum told Bustle in March 2024. "I wish that part didn’t happen. I feel like that kind of took on a life of its own. So that’s why I wanted to disappear. I was like, 'Unless there’s no story here, they’re not going to focus on just my work.'"Lohan moved abroad—first to London then to Dubai (also opening beach clubs in Greece). However, there was another reason she sought a life away from the spotlight.

"I was like, 'What if I never fall in love? What if this never happens?'" she added. "And it took me just taking time for me for all those doors to open and the ‘yeses’ to come—the things I wanted to say 'yes' to."Of course, Lohan did find love with Bader Shammas, the pair marrying in 2022 and welcoming son Luai the following year. They still live in Dubai, but the Freaky Friday actress hasn't left the Hollywood industry completely, starring in movies like Our Little Secret, Irish Wish and Freakier Friday.

For Hartnett, the decision to leave Hollywood came after some self-reflection."Hollywood is more than a place; it's like a state of mind," the Black Mirror actor told People in July 2024. "If you're around people who are constantly talking about the movie business, your life is going to be pretty much one note. And I've never wanted that."Instead, he wanted more."I've always wanted to be around ... people generally doing lots of other things that would bring my mind off of my work and force me to grow in different directions," Hartnett added. "To me, that's the spice of life."So, the Black Hawk Down alum, his wife Tamsin Egerton and their four kids moved to England's Hampshire countryside."Time passes quickly," he told The Guardian in July 2024. "With four children, you have so much to do. In a way, less is happening. But more of the important stuff is happening."Still, Hartnett has stayed plenty busy and landed roles in Verity, Fight or Flight and Trap.

If you haven't checked your social network lately, then you might not know that Eisenberg doesn't live in L.A."I’ve lived in Indiana for the last decade on-and-off," the A Real Pain star told CBS News Sunday Morning in February 2025. "That’s where I feel the most comfortable. I’m not somebody who wants to surround myself in an industry that just feels kind of unstable to me."And while he's an Oscar nominee, he lives a pretty normal life with his wife Anna Strout and son Banner."I'm not on social media, and I'm not a person who's on the phone with industry people all the time," Eisenberg also shared. "So, my life feels pretty separate. My wife is a teacher. My kid doesn't really even watch movies. So, I'm not like knee-deep in the world of constantly trying to assess my own status in an industry."

After appearing in such projects as Buffy the Vampire Slayer and 2000's Bring It On, Dushku revealed in September 2024 that she had become certified in psychedelic-assisted therapy and is furthering her studies as a mental health professional.

"I had the means to shift directions and choose a course in my life that focused on healing myself so that I could help heal others," she told Boston Magazine. "I would be remiss if I didn’t now share the transformation and the peace and the passion that I have. This is just absolutely so clearly my real calling, my real purpose."

The Flintstones star revealed that she moved to Ireland in January 2025 with her youngest child Clay and was in the process of getting her Irish citizenship as her grandparents are from the European country. But while Rosie cited recent political developments as her reason for leaving, she didn’t rule out an eventual return home.

"I miss my other kids," she said in a video on TikTok. "I miss my friends. I miss many things about life there at home and I'm trying to find a home here in in this beautiful country. And when it is safe for all citizens to have equal rights there in America, that's when we will consider coming back."

The Ant-Man and the Wasp star announced she's taking an indefinite hiatus from acting after 20 years in the industry.

"I am so filled with joy and contentment today as I live out my vision," Lilly wrote on Instagram in June 2024. "I feel so grateful for my blessings. Stepping away from what seems like the obvious choice (wealth and fame) can feel scary at times, but stepping into your dharma replaces the fear with fulfillment."

But she isn't necessarily shutting the door, either, adding, "I might return to Hollywood one day, but, for now, this is where I belong."

The Vampire Diaries alum hasn't sunk his teeth into a new role since Netflix's 2019 series V-Wars. Instead, he has dug a little deeper into a passion project, namely his mission to combat climate change by improving the world's soil.

"I stepped away from acting a little over four years ago to raise my kids, build my companies and get these films launched," Somerhalder, who shares two children with wife Nikki Reed, told E! News in November 2023 of launching the 2020 documentary Kiss the Ground and its follow up Common Ground, each detailing the need for regenerative farming.

When he looks years down the road, the actor continued, "I will be a rancher and building legacy brands, whether it's my bourbon or my health and wellness company, and the regenerative agriculture and healthy soil management practices that I live by and our family lives by. That's where my life was going. So when people say 'Why do you care?' That's why I care. Because that's who I am, that's what I'm going to become."

On a February 2021 episode of her podcast Empty Inside, the iCarly alum told guest Anna Faris that she decided to stop acting a few years back and is now focused on opportunities in writing and directing, in addition to hosting the podcast.

"My experience with acting is, I'm so ashamed of the parts I've done in the past," revealed McCurdy, who detailed her experience in her 2022 memoir I'm Glad My Mom Died. "I resent my career in a lot of ways. I feel so unfulfilled by the roles that I played and felt like it was the most cheesy, embarrassing. I did the shows that I was on from like 13 to 21, and by 15, I was already embarrassed. My friends at 15, they're not like, 'Oh, cool, you're on this Nickelodeon show.' It was embarrassing."

Though she hasn't totally written off a second act. "I do feel like only through writing the book have I gotten to a place where I think there might be a way of exploring acting that doesn't carry that baggage that I carried with me for so long," she told E! News in October 2022. "Maybe if I write something for myself. I think that'd really be maybe one of the only ways I could kind of try exploring it again."

This felt like something of a no-brainer. If we had a shot to marry Prince Harry, dedicate our life to the philanthropic causes that matter most to us and gain access to the Queen's impressive collection of tiaras, bidding ta-ta to Tinseltown would feel like an okay sacrifice.

Following the path Grace Kelly took from Hollywood to the Palace of Monaco, Meghan left behind her home in Toronto—and her breakout role on Suits—for a life in The Firm. Though, now that she and Harry have shed their senior roles and live in Montecito, Calif., she's edging back into the business thanks to business moves like their multi-year production deal with Netflix. The Duchess of Sussex released her 2022 docuseries Harry & Meghan as well as her 2025 lifestyle show With Love, Meghan on the streaming service. She's also launched podcasts and her brand As Ever.

Having made upwards of 40 movies since her debut in 1994's The Mask, the actress was long overdue for a break when filming wrapped on 2014's Annie.

"I just decided that I wanted different things out of my life," she explained to pal Gwyneth Paltrow of her ultimate act of self-care. "I had gone so hard for so long, working, making films and it's such a grind. When you're making a movie—it's a perfect excuse—they own you. You're there for 12 hours a day for months on end and you have no time for anything else."

And there was plenty more she'd like to explore, from writing (she followed up her 2013 New York Times best-seller The Body Book with 2016's The Longevity Book) to starting a family with husband Benji Madden. But while Cameron confessed to InStyle in 2019, "I don't miss performing. Right now I'm looking at the landscape of wellness and all that," apparently she could be swayed.

"We just begged and pleased on my knees, like, 'Just give the people one more again,'" Jamie Foxx told E! News of getting Diaz to sign on for the 2025 Netflix film Back in Action. "We love her, we've been waiting on her and this is just gonna be fantastic."

The actor insisted there'd be no encore after he finished his five-year run on Empire. When Extra asked Howard about his future ahead of the musical drama series' sixth and final season in 2019, he responded, "Oh, I'm done with acting. I'm done pretending."

And though he returned to set for a handful of projects, the Oscar nominee again announced his plans to quit acting while promoting his Peacock series The Best Man: The Final Chapters in 2022. "I've gotten to the point where now I've given the very best that I have as an actor," he told ET. "Now I'm enjoying watching other new talent come around, and I don't want to do an impersonation of myself."

Despite these comments, though, Howard has since appeared in a few more shows and movies, including the TV series Fight Night: The Million Dollar Heist and Netflix film Shirley, with multiple projects lined up in the future.

Once his time as King Joffrey came to a sudden, purple-faced end in 2014, the then-21-year-old told EW he was getting out of the game. "I've been acting since age 8," the Game of Thrones star explained of his decision. "I just stopped enjoying it as much as I used to."

No longer a child star, a bit of the magic had worn off. "Now there's the prospect of doing it for a living, whereas up until now it was always something I did for recreation with my friends, or in the summer for some fun," Gleeson continued. "I enjoyed it. When you make a living from something, it changes your relationship with it. It's not like I hate it, it's just not what I want to do."

But after a six-year break, he was ready to resume his reign, joining the cast of BBC's series Out of Her Mind in 2020. Since then, Jack has also appeared in movies like Rebecca's Boyfriend and In the Land of Saints and Sinners as well as TV shows like Safe Harbor and The Famous Five.

When Fast Times at Ridgemont High's dream girl (Jennifer Aniston took on her part in September 2020's virtual table read) wed fellow actor Kevin Kline in 1989, they "agreed to alternate so that we're never working at the same time," he told Playboy of their plan to care for son Owen and daughter Greta (a singer who now goes by the stage name Frankie Cosmos).

However, he continued, "whenever it's been her slot to work, Cates has chosen to stay with the children." Though she made a cameo in pal Jennifer Jason Leigh's 2001 indie The Anniversary Party, Phoebe devotes most of her time to operating her New York City boutique Blue Tree.

At the height of his Ghostbusters and Honey, I... fame, the '80s star stepped away from filmmaking not long after his wife passed away from breast cancer in 1991 to focus on raising his kids Rachel and Mitchell.

Though Moranis hasn't had a live-action movie role since 1997, even passing on a cameo in Paul Feig's 2016 Ghostbusters remake, he's remained a treasured cultural icon, as evidenced by the outrage over reports that he'd been assaulted while walking in New York City in 2020.Thankfully there's good news for fans: He'll make his triumphant return alongside Josh Gad in the forthcoming Disney reboot Shrunk.

Once she wed fashion designer Adam Kimmel in 2010, the Never Been Kissed standout hinted that she was maybe kinda done with movies. "Ninety percent of acting roles involve so much sexual stuff with other people, and I don't want to do that," she explained to Vogue. "It's such a strange fire to play with, and our relationship is surely strong enough to handle it, but if you're going to walk through fire, there has to be something incredible on the other side."

Her decision was solidified after son Martin joined older sister Louisanna in 2014. "I don't do movie stuff anymore. I am totally an outsider! I … am just a mom and an outsider," she noted to Us Weekly at a 2016 event, explaining that she helps Kimmel with his business and paints on the side. "I am just focused on my kids. I think that's mainly why I stopped."

She'd done Ally McBeal. And Nip/Tuck. Then Arrested Development and finally Scandal when the Aussie realized that maybe she was ready to turn the dial.

"I was approaching 45 and I just kind of…was wondering is there something that I could tackle now that I've never done before that would be really challenging and different," she explained on wife Ellen DeGeneres' eponymous talk show in 2018. "I kind of knew what acting would look like for me for the next 10, 20 years, so I decided to quit and start a business."

Her consumer-art company, General Public, already a work in progress, she had just one piece to finish.

"I called Mitch Hurwitz, who's the creator of Arrested Development and I said, 'If there is a season 5, I won't be doing it because I quit acting. And he seemed really understanding and he totally got it. We had a great conversation, and then he wrote me into five episodes."

To be fair, once you've won three Academy Awards, what's left to accomplish? Shortly after receiving his sixth Oscar nod for his final film, 2017's Phantom Thread, the thespian had his rep issue a statement informing fans that he "will no longer be working as an actor. He is immensely grateful to all of his collaborators and audiences over the many years. This is a private decision and neither he nor his representatives will make any further comment on this subject."

But just when Day-Lewis thought he was out, his son pulled him back in. In October 2024, production company Focus Features announced the Oscar winner would star in 2025's Anemone, the film he wrote alongside son Ronan Day-Lewis.

The Good Luck Charlie alum took a step back from the spotlight in 2018 when she began pursuing a master's degree from MIT, later earning a PhD from the institution. She also enrolled in Harvard Law School.

And as if that weren't enough, Mendler launched her own startup Northwood Space, which aims to build ground satellite stations to help send and receive data from space, becoming CEO of the brand in February 2023.

For Artemis II astronaut Victor Glover, one of the hardest parts of traveling to the moon happened before he even left Earth.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

TENERIFE, Canary Islands — Former NASA astronaut Victor Glover has flown in combat, performed four spacewalks and strapped himself to the top of rockets launching into space. But before embarking on his historic Artemis II journey around the moon, he faced something even more difficult: a conversation with his four daughters.

Speaking alongside former astronaut Chris Hadfield at the Starmus VIII festival in Tenerife, Canary Islands, on Oct. 18, Glover opened up about the challenges of preparing his family for his riskiest mission yet.

"This is maybe the greatest challenge of my astronaut career," Glover said.

Glover joined NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman and Christina Koch and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen aboard NASA's Artemis II mission, which launched on April 1, 2026, marking humanity's first crewed journey to the moon since Apollo 17 in 1972.

But preparing for the historic journey wasn't just about mastering the spacecraft and executing the mission successfully. It also meant making sure his family was ready for what lay ahead.

When Glover first traveled to space aboard SpaceX's Crew-1 mission in 2020, his children were much younger and he and his wife, Dionna, made a conscious effort to prepare them for his time in space.

"We decided, as a parental unit, Dionna and I, that we were going to put as much effort into making sure our family was ready as NASA was putting into making sure I was ready to be a crew member," Glover explained.

The family visited NASA's Kennedy Space Center, toured the launch pad and crew quarters and even planned when Glover would call home from the International Space Station. But by the time Artemis II came around, things were different. All four of his daughters were now adults, and preparing them for his journey around the moon meant discussing the mission's risks, including the possibility that he might not return home.

Glover recalled his wife telling him something he described as maybe the scariest thing he'd ever heard.

"You should have this talk with our daughters."

And although he knew she was right, it wasn't an easy conversation to have.

"We did, and it did not go well in my opinion," Glover admitted. "Well, it's not about going well. The talk needed to be done, just because it's hard."

The following day, Glover sent his daughters and wife a poem, Live Your Life, by Chief Tecumseh.

The poem helped Glover express something he had struggled to put into words during their conversation: why he believed the risks of traveling to the moon were worth taking.

"It was a very tough conversation, but they understood that I know this is risky. I wasn't just telling them Dad's risking his life. There's a real point to this and there's a reason to take this risk," Glover explained. "This poem helped me to say it in a way that I didn't have words for."

After traveling around the moon and returning safely to Earth, one moment stood out above all others. When we asked Glover in a separate interview at Starmus on Oct. 20, which moment from Artemis II he would most like to relive, he answered immediately.

"It's the true, ultimate mission accomplishment. Just 'we did it.' We survived. My family is relieved, and there's just nothing like it," Glover explained. "There's nothing like coming home. There's nothing like returning to Earth."

She also has a keen interest in astrotourism and is always on the lookout for the next northern lights adventure.

She will join Hurtigruten as an onboard astronomer for a northern lights sailing in January 2027.

#797. Alzheimer’s may have early warning signs outside the brain

Alzheimer's disease is best known for its effects on memory and thinking, but new research suggests that some symptoms may develop in a surprising place: outside the brain.

Scientists at the University of Central Florida (UCF) have discovered that genetic mutations associated with Alzheimer's can interfere with the nerves that control muscle movement, even without involvement from the brain or spinal cord. The findings could help explain why some people with Alzheimer's experience changes in walking, balance, or coordination long before noticeable memory problems emerge.

The discovery raises the possibility that movement difficulties could provide earlier warning signs of the disease and that treatments focused exclusively on the brain may overlook important problems elsewhere in the body.

The research was led by James Hickman, a professor at UCF's Nanoscience Technology Center, and Research Professor Xiufang "Nadine" Guo, working alongside scientists at the healthcare technology company Hesperos. Funded by the National Institutes of Health's National Institute on Aging, the study used laboratory systems built from human cells to investigate how inherited Alzheimer's mutations affect movement. The findings were published in Alzheimer's & Dementia: The Journal of the Alzheimer's Association.

"Motor deficits may be an earlier indication [of Alzheimer's]," Guo says. "If we can detect those changes and intervene earlier, that could help delay the onset of central nervous system symptoms."

Why Alzheimer's Symptoms May Appear Before Memory Loss

Alzheimer's is generally associated with progressive memory loss, confusion, and declining cognitive abilities. However, doctors have also observed that some patients develop physical symptoms, including changes in balance, coordination, and gait (manner of walking), years before clear cognitive difficulties become apparent.

These observations have raised an important question: Are such movement problems simply a consequence of damage occurring in the brain, or could Alzheimer's also interfere directly with nerves elsewhere in the body?

To investigate, the UCF team focused on familial Alzheimer's, a rare inherited form of the disease that typically develops earlier in life (from 40 to 65 years of age) than the more common form.

Their experiments revealed that motor neurons carrying mutations linked to familial Alzheimer's could disrupt the connections responsible for controlling muscles, even when the brain and spinal cord were completely absent from the experimental system.

Motor neurons are specialized nerve cells that transmit signals to muscles, telling them when to contract and produce movement. The new findings suggest that Alzheimer's mutations can interfere with this process directly, rather than affecting movement only through damage to the brain.

"This is the first time it's been demonstrated that deficits in the peripheral nervous system can arise directly from these mutations," Hickman says. "It means drugs that target the brain may not fix problems in the rest of the body."

The peripheral nervous system includes the nerves located outside the brain and spinal cord. These nerves carry signals between the central nervous system and the rest of the body, helping control movement, sensation, and other essential functions.

Guo also points out that preserving the ability to move could have benefits beyond physical health. Regular physical activity is associated with better cognitive well-being, so protecting motor function may also help support brain health.

How a Miniature Human Cell System Revealed the Discovery

To examine the relationship between Alzheimer's mutations and muscle movement, the scientists used an innovative laboratory platform known as "human-on-a-chip" technology.

Developed and manufactured through Hesperos, a company co-founded by Hickman, these miniature systems bring different types of human cells together under controlled conditions. They allow researchers to recreate specific biological functions and observe how diseases interfere with them.

Unlike conventional laboratory experiments that examine isolated cells, these systems can reproduce important interactions between different tissues. They also provide an alternative to animal models, which do not always accurately reflect how human diseases behave.

For this study, the team created a miniature model of the neuromuscular junction, the connection where a motor neuron communicates with a muscle cell.

The model was deliberately designed without a brain or spinal cord. This was a crucial part of the experiment because it allowed the researchers to investigate whether Alzheimer's-related changes could cause movement problems independently of the central nervous system.

The scientists combined healthy muscle cells with motor neurons derived from stem cells that carried genetic mutations associated with familial Alzheimer's disease. Stem cells are cells that can develop into specialized types of cells, making them valuable tools for studying human diseases in the laboratory.

The researchers then examined how effectively the altered nerve cells communicated with otherwise healthy muscle tissue.

The results showed that the Alzheimer's-associated mutations could interfere with normal nerve-to-muscle function. This suggests that at least some movement difficulties linked to the disease may arise directly in the peripheral nervous system rather than being caused entirely by degeneration in the brain.

Why Damaged Nerve Connections Can Affect Walking and Balance

Every voluntary movement depends on successful communication between the nervous system and the muscles.

At the neuromuscular junction, an electrical signal traveling along a motor neuron triggers chemical communication that causes a muscle to contract. This process makes everyday activities possible, from walking and maintaining posture to lifting objects and performing precise movements.

When the connection becomes impaired, muscles may respond less effectively to nerve signals. Depending on the severity and location of the problem, this can contribute to weakness, reduced coordination, and difficulty sustaining physical activity.

To evaluate these effects, the research team measured how consistently nerve signals produced muscle contractions and how long the muscles could continue contracting before becoming fatigued.

These measurements provided a direct assessment of how well the nerve and muscle cells worked together. They also resemble aspects of the functional testing physicians use when examining patients with movement disorders.

"You can't move unless the motor circuit works," Hickman says. "When a doctor taps your knee to check your reflex, they're testing that exact connection."

By demonstrating impaired nerve-to-muscle communication in a system containing no brain or spinal cord, the study provides evidence that mutations linked to familial Alzheimer's can produce effects beyond the central nervous system.

However, the experiments do not establish that these changes necessarily occur before memory loss in patients. Further research will be needed to determine how closely the laboratory findings reflect the progression of Alzheimer's in people, particularly those with the more common forms of the disease.

Could This Discovery Lead to Earlier Alzheimer's Detection?

The findings suggest a potentially important new direction for Alzheimer's research: looking beyond memory and other cognitive symptoms when investigating the disease.

If future studies confirm that changes in motor function are detectable early in certain patients, tests of walking, coordination, or nerve-to-muscle activity might eventually help identify disease-related changes before more obvious neurological symptoms develop.

The results also raise questions about treatment. Many Alzheimer's therapies are designed to address processes occurring in the brain, but medications that target the central nervous system may not necessarily correct abnormalities affecting peripheral nerves and muscles.

Understanding these separate effects could help researchers investigate treatments that protect physical function alongside cognitive health.

Human-on-a-Chip Technology Could Transform Disease Research

Beyond the implications for Alzheimer's, the researchers see considerable potential in using human-on-a-chip systems to investigate other diseases and evaluate possible treatments.

Because these platforms contain human cells and reproduce measurable biological activities, they can help scientists observe disease-related changes in conditions that more closely resemble human physiology than some conventional experimental models.

This approach may be particularly useful in drug development, where researchers need to understand not only how a potential treatment affects individual cells but also how it influences interactions between different tissues.

Such systems can also uncover biological effects that may be difficult to detect in animal experiments, potentially helping researchers identify promising therapies and recognize limitations earlier in development.

For Hickman, the progress represents the culmination of three decades of work devoted to understanding disease through more realistic laboratory models.

"These systems let us study disease in a way that's closer to what actually happens in the human body, and that's what we need to develop better treatments," he says.

#796. London City's Goodwin gets first England call-up

Izzy Goodwin has scored three goals in five WSL appearances for London City

London City Lionesses forward Izzy Goodwin has been named in the England squad for the first time for the World Cup qualifying play-off against Ukraine.

The 23-year-old has been in great form this month and scored in front of England manager Sarina Wiegman at Emirates Stadium on Sunday in a 1-1 draw with Arsenal.

"We have always seen her as a huge talent with potential," Wiegman told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"I think London City are developing really well in the games they have showed. She is tall and can head a ball attacking-wise, but also defending.

"She is really quick with her feet and can score goals. I really want to see her in our environment, what she can bring and how close she is to the level that we expect."

There is also a first call-up for goalkeeper Katie Cox, on loan at Nottingham Forest from Chelsea, while Manchester United midfielder Ella Toone returns.

Manchester City duo Niamh Charles and Alex Greenwood, who is injured, are among those to miss out.

The Lionesses play Ukraine in Spain on 1 December before hosting them at Wembley on 5 December. The winner qualifies for next year's Women's World Cup.

"We know what's at stake in these games and our focus is on producing two strong performances to secure our place at the World Cup," said Wiegman.

"We have worked hard to put ourselves in this position and now we have to finish the job.

"Ukraine will provide a challenge and we will prepare with the same focus and determination that we always do."

Chelsea defender Lucy Bronze could make her 150th appearance at Wembley in the second leg.

England travel to Pinatar, Spain a few days before the first leg and opted not to play a friendly match during this extended international break.

"The first part of the block we are [at St George's Park]. We have training sessions and a period of time where we can do some tactical stuff," added Wiegman.

"We also selected more players so that helps us create situations where we can train things and everyone is important. I'm really excited to get ready for these games."

Sarina Wiegman led England to victory at Euro 2022 and Euro 2025

Wiegman was speaking to media at St George's Park for the first time since signing a new contract that will run until the end of Euro 2029.

It means she could oversee England's fortunes at next year's World Cup if they beat Ukraine, as well as heading up a Team GB squad at the 2028 Olympic Games.

Asked why she wanted to extend her stay, Wiegman told BBC Radio 5 Live: "Well, first of all the FA is happy with me and I'm really happy with them.

"I'm really grateful for that environment. That is one [reason]. Secondly, I still feel a great connection with staff and players, and of course the country!

"Then we have the challenges ahead. The major tournaments always motivate me. You don't get many moments with the team because it's not like it is at a club.

"In a tournament, you have those moments where you are really together, you can get somewhere with the group and that really excites me.

"Yes, the Olympics would be really great. Next year it's the World Cup, then it's the Olympics, then it's the Euros â that journey ahead really excites me."

Wiegman's contract renewal was kept under wraps and it came as a surprise following their two-legged victory over Greece in October.

The Dutchwoman, who has guided England to successive European titles, said conversations had been ongoing for a while but she had not planned ahead.

"When I signed that first contract in 2020 to join in 2021, it was a four-year contract and I thought, 'ok, this is a long contract, it would be really great if things go well'.

"We all got so excited so I signed another contract until 2027 and now I have until 2029. That is eight years. I never expected that. I also never planned so far ahead.

"I want to feel that I can contribute to the environment and the development of things. I also want that from the other party. You want it to fit and for it to work.

"That decision came over time. At one point you think: 'Yeah, I'm getting really excited again.' That is what you want. To feel the energy, to feel the excitement.

"I still think we have things we can improve. We know the game is improving so quickly so we have to adapt all the time. When you stand still, you are lost."

Wiegman is also determined to improve as a coach and has enjoyed overseeing the development of younger talent as the Lionesses transition.

"It starts with me and about how I am going to develop. I keep learning things about myself too. You need to know yourself really well to do this job," she added.

"The staff and the players will always challenge me in the right ways. It goes back and forth. That is what I want. I really want to improve myself all the time."

#795. Queen Mary of Denmark Gives Update on Queen Margrethe After Death Hoax

Queen Mary of Denmark spoke out about her mother-in-law Queen Margrethe's health after the former monarch—who abdicated the throne in favor of son King Frederik—became the subject of a death hoax.

Queen Mary of Denmark will not give gossip the royal treatment.

After her mother-in-law Queen Margrethe II—who broke a 900-year tradition in 2024 by abdicating the throne in favor of son King Frederik X—recently became the subject of a death hoax, the 54-year-old spoke out to address the former sovereign's health.

As Mary attended the Children's Aid Day Awards in Copenhagen Nov. 17, she told reporters, according to Hello, that Margrethe "is resting at home."

Her comment echoed an earlier statement from the Amalienborg Palace, which had announced on the same day that Margrethe had canceled her appearance at a separate public engagement due to a sore throat.

“Her Majesty is now at Fredensborg Palace," a Nov. 17 press release stated, "and is doing well, given the circumstances."

As for what initially sparked concerns over Margrethe's health? That all had to do with an obituary that was accidentally published by Danish outlet TV2 Fyn on Nov. 13.

"Denmark has lost a queen," the article's subheading read, according to Hello. "A person who, throughout her life, united regions and generations, and played a special role for the people of Funen."

The publication's editor-in-chief Thomas Funding later apologized for the gaffe, calling it an "unfortunate mistake."

The accidental publishing came two months after Margrethe was hospitalized for the third time this year. The four-day stay at the Rigshospitalet hospital, which the palace said was for a "blood clot in the hip region and mild dehydration," led her to miss a state funeral for state funeral of King Harald of Norway.

"Queen Margrethe is in good spirits and, given the circumstances, is doing well," Danish royal officials said at the time, adding upon Margrethe's discharge that she "will take it easy in the coming time."

For more recent new about royal families around the world, read on.

Kate Middleton & Prince William's Son Prince George Starts School at Eton College

On Sept. 8, the Prince and Princess of Wales' oldest son started his first day of school at Eton College, a boarding school Prince William attended in his youth.

Prince Harry, Meghan Markle Return to U.K. for Extended Stay

King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV Dies at 34

Meghan Markle's Show With Love, Meghan Scores Daytime Emmy Nomination

On July 7, British Justice Matthew Nicklin ruled against a group of high profile figures—including the Duke of Sussex, Elton John and Elizabeth Hurley—in a lawsuit accusing the Associated Newspapers, the publisher of the Daily Mail, of unlawful information gathering.

Prince William and Kate Middleton Break Silence on the Epstein Files

Marius Borg Høiby, Son of Norway's Crown Princess, Arrested Ahead of Rape Trial

Marius Borg Høiby—the eldest son of Crown Princess Mette-Marit and step-son of Crown Prince Haakon—was arrested Feb. 1 for assault, threats with a knife and violation of a restraining order, Oslo police confirmed in a statement to The Associated Press.

The 29-year-old—who does not carry a royal title or official duties—is being kept in detention for up to four weeks over risks of reoffending after the Oslo district court granted the request. His attorney Petar Sekulic told the outlet that they are considering appealing the decision.

Høiby is expected in court Feb. 3 as part of a separate indictment regarding four alleged rapes between 2018 and 2024, as well as two alleged acts of violence against a partner and violating a restraining order.

Flora Vesterberg, Queen Elizabeth's Cousin, Announces Pregnancy

Set to Olivia Dean’s “So Easy (To Fall In Love),” the couple revealed that the clip was recorded by none other than their 4-year-old daughter Lilibet.  Alongside a camera emoji, Meghan—who also shares 6-year-old son Archie with Harry— added in the caption of the Jan. 16 Instagram post, “cred: our daughter.”

Kate Middleton Celebrates Her Birthday With Moving Message

“Even in the coldest, darkest season, winter has a way of bringing us stillness, patience and quiet consideration,” Kate said in a voiceover alongside footage of snowy landscapes in her Jan. 9 video. “Where the stream slows just enough for us to see our own reflection, to discover the deepest parts of ourselves, alongside the whispers and the pulse of every living thing.”

She added, “I find myself reflecting on how deeply grateful I am. For the rivers within us flow with ease, fears washed away, cleanse and purify, come to peace with our tears and discover what it means to be alive, to be at one with nature—a quiet teacher and a soft voice that guides in memory helping us to heal in.”

Kate Middleton Makes Surprise Appearance With Prince William

#793. Ronaldo, Maradona, Baggio - what happened to the World XI?

Soren Colding wasn't expecting the call. "The Laudrup brothers, Peter Schmeichel, there might have been some cancellations," he jokes.

Eventually, the Danish FA turned to a Brondby defender who had played a handful of times for the national team.

The assignment? He would be expected to mark Ronaldo and Gabriel Batistuta as part of a Europe XI against the Rest of the World at Marseille's Velodrome.

It was December 1997, and Colding's team-mates would include defenders Fernando Hierro and Alessandro Costacurta, a midfield duo of Zinedine Zidane and Paul Ince, and Patrick Kluivert and Alen Boksic up top.

This was a star-sprinkled cast - one player from each of the competing nations at the following summer's World Cup joining forces before the draw took place.

"Of course, when you see those names, it was just more or less a dream come true," explains the Dane.

Colding was flown to France and chauffeured to the hotel. His driver offered to hang around in case the full-back fancied an impromptu shopping trip. There was no need. Instead, he discovered a bag of Fifa goodies in his room.

"There was the biggest Adidas bag I have ever seen in my life," he smiles. "I found a training suit and went down to lunch.

"Then I saw all the other guys on round tables - they were sitting with their agents, their wives, their family, their friends in normal [clothes]. Then the Danish guy turned in. Nobody knows who he is, in his Adidas training suit!"

Colding struck up a friendship with South Africa defender David Nyathi and the pair were whisked off to a 45-minute training session that afternoon. Not all the big names took part, but one Argentine offered a taste of what was to come.

"Batistuta was there and just to see him and his moves, you thought, 'Okay, it's gonna be a nice evening tomorrow'," remembers Colding, who also got to link up with European boss Franz Beckenbauer.

"He was pretty cool. He was saying, 'what is your position? Defender? OK, can you play left defender?' No problem - I'll play wherever you place me!"

Ronaldo scored twice and assisted three more goals as Rest of the World beat their Europe counterparts 5-2 in Marseille

Come game day, 38,000 fans packed in to see peak Ronaldo. Months earlier, Il Fenomeno completed a world-record move to Inter Milan on the back of 47 goals in 49 games in one sensational season at Barcelona.

The 21-year-old was the most exciting player on the planet.

"It was crazy, actually," recalls Colding, who previously faced the forward when Denmark's under-21s played Brazil in Florianopolis before the 1996 Olympics.

"That was almost the same team as they played with at the World Cup in '98. So we lost 5-1. Just to see his speed and how he played - I played against Roberto Carlos in that game as well - that was just another level. I thought, 'what is going on here?'

"When I saw him there again, it was just to see what is actually reachable for a football player, because that was next level tremendous. His speed and his touch are unbelievable, and also his power.

"And still, just a small, shy guy. You know, he just wants to play football, and all these people are around him protecting him. Just to see when a star like him joins an event like that, how many people around him, agents and followers, how should you navigate all that?"

Ronaldo, captaining Carlos Alberto Parreira's side, was at his blistering best, scoring twice and setting up the other three as Rest of the World won 5-2 - Batistuta also netted twice, before Zidane responded.

"You start thinking what if you injured some of them," explains Colding. "You are a defender, you don't want goals against you, so you have to fight - that's how I am.

"How hard should you go to them? Should you just let them go? No. I would not just let them run and score. I tried to do my best, that was probably not good enough!"

1987: Maradona stars in FA Centenary all-star game

This wasn't the first outing for a World XI, in fact such Fifa exhibition matches had been taking place since England hosted an all-star side in front of a reported 100,000 fans at Wembley in 1963 to celebrate the Football Association's centenary.

They became a semi-regular occurrence as testimonials or charity fixtures, with huge names appearing across eras from Eusebio and Zico to Roberto Baggio.

But the biggest coup was arguably luring Diego Maradona to Wembley a year after winning the World Cup with Argentina and scoring his 'Hand of God' goal against England.

Jon Smith, who represented the Napoli star, explains in his book 'The Deal' how Maradona was offered around Â£250,000 and flown from Naples on a private jet to take part in an anniversary game against the Football League.

"In fairness, he wanted to shake hands with the team and say 'sorry if I offended you'," Smith tells BBC Sport. "He genuinely believed his talent was God-given.

"He was sort of two people. He was lovely, Diego, when you were with him. When he crossed the white line he was Maradona. So the Hand of God was an expression of 'I am God's footballing representative', if you like.

"It was madness, because you can imagine how the media were all over it. It was a bit special."

Napoli and Argentina welcomed the opportunity for Maradona to generate some good PR in England, helped by Bobby Robson's Football League side winning 3-0 - Bryan Robson netting twice and Norman Whiteside grabbing the other.

"I remember introducing him to Bobby Robson," adds Smith. "He put his hand out, and Bobby said 'I'm not shaking that hand!', which I thought was lovely - he did shake the other hand!"

A Ronaldinho XI beat their Shevchenko counterparts 6-3 in February 2005 - Ronaldinho, Samuel Eto'o, Alessandro Del Piero and Gianfranco Zola were all on the scoresheet

One of the final games saw a Ronaldinho XI take on a Shevchenko XI at Nou Camp in February 2005 to raise funds for victims of the 2004 tsunami.

Andriy Shevchenko's stacked squad included Zidane, David Beckham, Alessandro Del Piero, Thierry Henry, Raul, Paolo Maldini and Steven Gerrard.

Ronaldinho could call on Ronaldo, Kaka, Cafu, Adriano, Javier Zanetti, Didier Drogba and Samuel Eto'o, though it was Southampton's Henri Camara who scored twice in a 6-3 win for the Brazilian's team.

But things have moved on, and it is hard to imagine clubs releasing their star players for such an exhibition nowadays.

"The whole world of football has changed," says Smith. "You used to have testimonial games and testimonial years because players got paid okay but by the same token weren't earning Â£100k a week.

"It wouldn't happen now because the business of football is so much bigger, you can't risk the players - if they get injured playing for their country, that annoys everybody.

"But beyond that they are owned by big corporations and in some cases countries, so you just wouldn't allow your player to go out and do that."

Colding went on to play 27 times for Denmark, featuring at the 1998 World Cup and Euro 2000, but retains fond memories of representing the Europe XI.

"Now, to come up with the idea to make a game like this, in combination with the draw, I think everyone will say you are crazy," explains Colding.

"But at that time it was perfectly planned and a fantastic event to be a part of. As players, we have a tremendous relationship between each other.

"It shows all the spectators you can be enemies on the field, but you can actually be friends and gather together in this kind of event.

"That for me sends a signal to all that we are a community in football and we can actually make great things together that not only is a question of money."

In fact, he still has his Europe shirt - a reminder of coming up against Ronaldo and Batistuta and being a team-mate of Zidane almost 30 years ago.

"It doesn't smell very good, actually," laughs Colding. "Sometimes, when I go in the garage with my kids and tell them about it and what actually happened, I see in their eyes, they don't really believe that I was a part of that game.

"That was not about money - we didn't get anything to join - it was just because you represent your country, so it was a great experience, it's also about having fun.

"You know, as small kids, you don't start by saying, 'I want to earn 20 million'. No, you start because it's fun to play football."

Soren Colding still has the shirt he wore for the Europe XI almost 30 years ago

#792. Scientists uncover a 192-year-old mystery hidden in a mangled silver coin

A badly distorted British silver coin dating to 1834 may hold evidence of an unusual accident during the minting process nearly 200 years ago. New scientific analysis suggests that the remarkable damage to the coin was more likely caused by a manufacturing problem than by ordinary wear, corrosion, or a later impact.

The findings, reported by IA STUDIO in the journal npj Heritage Science, center on a silver sixpence issued during the reign of King William IV. The coin was found in an album containing various coins at a car boot sale in Greater Manchester, England. Although the sixpence had an individual price tag of £8, the entire album was subsequently purchased as a single lot rather than the coin being bought separately.

What makes this particular sixpence remarkable is the extent and unusual pattern of its damage. Its central surface appears severely crushed and distorted, yet much of the outer rim and the small grooves along its edge remain relatively intact. The contrast raised an intriguing question about what could have happened to the coin.

To investigate, researchers examined the silver piece using powerful microscopes, chemical testing, and detailed three-dimensional surface measurements. The results point toward an unusual sequence of intense compression, potentially while the coin was being struck at the mint.

A Crushed Silver Coin Reveals Unusual Clues

The most striking evidence came from the coin's severely distorted central regions. Detailed measurements revealed deep, sharply defined depressions, elevated ridges, stepped surfaces, and areas where the metal appeared to have been pushed and displaced in overlapping patterns.

These features were particularly pronounced on the front of the coin, known as the obverse, which bears the portrait of William IV. Across the damaged central portrait area, the difference between the highest and lowest measured points reached approximately 0.75 millimeters.

That may sound small, but it represents a substantial distortion on the surface of a thin silver coin.

The investigators found that the overall damage was most consistent with repeated applications of high pressure concentrated in a limited area. The metal also appears to have been at least partly prevented from spreading outward as the force was applied.

This combination of heavy central damage and relatively well-preserved edges is difficult to reconcile with the gradual effects of circulation or simple corrosion. It also makes a single later impact, with the metal free to move outward, a less convincing explanation.

Instead, the findings favor an unusual problem during the original striking process, although the available evidence does not establish the exact sequence of events with certainty.

Microscopic Analysis Reveals Damage Beneath the Surface

To better understand the unusual deformation, the investigation combined scanning electron microscopy with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM-EDX) and optical surface profilometry.

The microscopic and chemical examinations provided information about the coin's metal composition and the changes affecting its surface.

In areas that had escaped the worst damage, testing identified an underlying silver and copper alloy. The more severely distorted regions contained lower measured concentrations of silver, higher levels of copper, and additional chemical evidence associated with corrosion and contamination.

These substances were especially concentrated inside the depressions formed by the damaged metal.

However, the chemical results largely reflected changes at the surface. Although corrosion and contamination had affected the coin, they could not adequately account for the depth, shape, and distribution of its unusual distortions.

The team also used optical surface profilometry, a technique that maps the height and shape of a surface in three dimensions. This made it possible to examine the coin's damaged areas in much greater detail than ordinary photographs could provide.

The resulting maps showed steep depressions, raised shoulders, abrupt changes in surface height, and multiple layers of metal displacement.

Using height measurements supplied by the Oxford Materials Characterisation Service, the study's author determined that the damaged central portrait region varied in height by approximately 750 micrometers, equivalent to 0.75 millimeters.

Taken together, the findings suggest that the coin underwent repeated compression while its sideways movement was at least partly restricted. This explanation fits the evidence better than ordinary wear, which generally smooths a coin's surface over time, or corrosion, which tends to remove or chemically alter material.

A Rare Glimpse Into 19th-Century Coin Production

The sixpence was produced in 1834, when Britain was already using steam-powered presses to manufacture coins.

During this period, coins with serious striking defects were typically identified through mint inspections and melted down so the metal could be reused. This was especially important for coins made from precious metals such as silver.

If the unusual deformation occurred during the original minting process, the sixpence may therefore represent a rare surviving example of a manufacturing failure that would ordinarily have been removed from circulation before it ever reached the public.

Such a coin could provide a physical record of a brief mechanical problem during the early era of mechanized coin production.

Determining whether the damage actually occurred at the mint is challenging, however. Historic metal objects can undergo many changes over decades or centuries, and severe deformation may obscure the physical clues needed to identify its origin.

To address this uncertainty, the study examined several kinds of evidence independently. The researchers considered the composition of the underlying metal, chemical changes at the surface, and the three-dimensional geometry of the deformation before comparing the results with different possible explanations.

The findings also demonstrate how non-destructive scientific techniques can be used to investigate other historic metal objects. By combining chemical and structural evidence, researchers may be able to distinguish manufacturing defects from later damage even when visual inspection alone provides no clear answer.

How AI Helped Investigate the Coin Mystery

The investigation also explored how computational tools, including artificial intelligence, could assist in evaluating a historical mystery without replacing physical scientific evidence.

Before any laboratory results were available, the author began by studying high-resolution photographs of the sixpence and systematically reviewing its unusual surface features.

This early examination helped identify several possible causes of the damage and establish what kinds of physical measurements would be needed to test them.

Human-supervised computational tools, including large language models (LLMs), helped organize the observations, develop alternative explanations, compare competing ideas, and formulate questions that could later be investigated through laboratory testing.

Importantly, the initial hypotheses and analytical notes were recorded before the independently produced laboratory measurements became available.

The possible explanations included ordinary circulation wear and corrosion, mechanical damage occurring after minting, later compression under restricted conditions, and deformation during the original manufacturing process.

To investigate these possibilities, independent measurements were commissioned from the Experimental Techniques Centre at Brunel University of London and the Oxford Materials Characterisation Service within the Department of Materials at the University of Oxford.

Once the testing was completed, computational tools were used again to help organize the resulting data and compare the physical findings with the earlier explanations.

"The important sequence was hypothesis first, independent laboratory measurement second," said A. Ikraam, founder of IA STUDIO and author of the study.

"We used the models to ask what features mattered and what evidence could distinguish one explanation from another. Then the laboratory measurements gave us something physical to test those ideas against. The models could support the reasoning process, but they could not decide what happened to the coin."

Scientific Evidence Points to a Possible Minting Error

Although artificial intelligence played a supporting role in organizing observations and evaluating competing possibilities, it did not produce the laboratory measurements or determine the final findings.

The study's conclusions were based on independently generated scientific data, with the author retaining responsibility for interpreting the evidence and deciding which explanation was best supported.

The results favor a rare minting anomaly involving repeated, highly concentrated pressure, rather than damage caused by ordinary circulation, corrosion, or a single unrestricted impact after production. Nevertheless, the research does not conclusively establish every detail of what happened to the sixpence.

Beyond shedding light on the possible origins of a strangely mangled 1834 coin, the investigation illustrates how modern imaging, chemical analysis, and carefully evaluated computational tools can work together to uncover clues hidden in historic objects.

What initially appeared to be little more than a badly damaged silver coin may instead preserve an unusual record of how something went wrong during the early days of mechanized coin manufacturing.

#790. What exactly is a light-day? Here's what Voyager 1's latest milestone means for the interstellar probe

The record highlights the enormous distances involved in deep-space exploration.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

After nearly 50 years traveling through space, NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is approaching a milestone no human-made object has reached before: a distance of one light-day from Earth.

This milestone — which Voyager 1 is expected to reach on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026, at 5:16:07 a.m. EST (1016:07 GMT) — highlights the immense distances Voyager 1 has traveled and the challenges of communicating with spacecraft operating in the outer reaches of the solar system and beyond.

Astronomers use a measurement known as a light-day to describe how far light travels in 24 hours. Light moves at approximately 186,000 miles (300,000 kilometers) per second, meaning one light-day is roughly 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers), according to a statement from NASA.

Although the term light-day might sound like a measurement of time, it is actually a unit of distance, much like a light-year. Astronomers use light-based measurements because conventional miles and kilometers become increasingly difficult to comprehend when describing the enormous distances between objects in space.

For perspective on how far Voyager 1 has travelled, sunlight takes about eight minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth, meaning our planet is approximately 8.3 light-minutes from the sun. Radio signals traveling between Earth and Mars can take anywhere from three to 22 minutes, depending on the planets' positions in their orbits, according to the statement.

By comparison, when Voyager 1 reaches one light-day from Earth, a radio signal sent from the probe will take a full 24 hours to reach mission controllers on Earth, and a command transmitted from Earth will take another 24 hours to reach the spacecraft.

The communication delay affects how engineers operate spacecraft at such distances. Unlike spacecraft operating closer to Earth, which can receive commands and return data with relatively little delay, communicating with Voyager 1 requires mission controllers to account for the extended signal travel time when planning spacecraft operations, troubleshooting technical issues and evaluating the results of commands sent to the probe.

Voyager 1 has been traveling away from Earth since its launch on Sept. 5, 1977. Now cruising through interstellar space at nearly 38,000 mph (61,000 kph), the spacecraft has spent more than 49 years covering the distance that light can cross in a single day.

Even at that speed, Voyager 1 is moving relatively slowly compared with light itself. Its twin, Voyager 2, which launched in 1977 on a different trajectory, is expected to reach the same one-light-day milestone in November 2035.

As Voyager 1 and, eventually, Voyager 2 continue their journeys through interstellar space, their growing distances from Earth offer a measure of both the reach of human exploration and the communication challenges that come with sending spacecraft ever farther into the cosmos.

Samantha Mathewson joined Space.com as an intern in the summer of 2016. She received a B.A. in Journalism and Environmental Science at the University of New Haven, in Connecticut. Previously, her work has been published in Nature World News. When not writing or reading about science, Samantha enjoys traveling to new places and taking photos!
